title: Could the Irish Miracle be Repeated in Hungary?
summary_en: Could Hungary replicate Ireland's economic miracle? Ács, O'Gorman, Szerb and Terjesen use Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) data to compare entrepreneurial activity in the two countries shortly after Hungary's EU accession. They find significant differences in the type of people starting businesses and the opportunities pursued — Ireland's growth was associated with high-quality opportunity-driven entrepreneurship, while Hungary's pattern was more necessity-driven. The policy prescription for Hungary: focus on raising human capital, promoting enterprise development, and upgrading the quality of FDI rather than just attracting more of it.
data_used: Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) survey data on ~2,000 Hungarian and ~2,000 Irish adults, including new-firm founders and prospective entrepreneurs, mid-2000s. Includes type of entrepreneurial activity (necessity vs. opportunity) and motivations.
policy_relevance: Direct historical comparison addressing a foundational Hungarian policy question. The paper's policy prescription — quality-of-FDI over quantity-of-FDI, plus human-capital and enterprise-development investment — has remained relevant through HIPA's evolution and the post-2010 reindustrialisation strategy. Useful for KKM, Pénzügyminisztérium, and ITM when re-evaluating long-term FDI-promotion frameworks.

title: Entrepreneurship, Economic Growth and Public Policy
summary_en: Ács and Szerb's introduction to the second Global Entrepreneurship Research Conference draws together cross-country evidence on the entrepreneurship-growth-policy relationship. They argue that the appropriate entrepreneurship policy depends on a country's stage of development. Middle-income countries (including Hungary) should focus on raising human capital, upgrading technology availability, and promoting enterprise development. Developed economies, by contrast, may not see more high-potential startups simply from reducing entry regulations — labour-market reform and financial-market deregulation may be needed.
data_used: Cross-country meta-review of papers in the Small Business Economics special issue (2007) using Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) micro and macro data, covering 30+ countries at varying development stages.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungary's evolving entrepreneurship-policy framework. The paper supports the case that Hungary, as a middle-income economy, should prioritise human-capital and technology-upgrading investments over deregulation. Useful framing for ITM, Pénzügyminisztérium, and Hungarian academic institutions when designing the Hungarian National Smart Specialisation Strategy.

title: Infrastruktúra-bővítés világversenyek idején. A Mol Bubi esete a FINA világbajnoksággal
summary_en: Should bike-share networks expand based on the demand of the existing service or based on hosting one-off mega-events? Bakó, Berezvai, Cseke and Isztin study Budapest's Mol Bubi expansion built for the 17th FINA Aquatic World Championships. Using event-study and difference-in-differences methods, they compare post-event utilisation of the FINA-related new docks with that of earlier expansion docks. The new docks become an organic part of the network but their utilisation is substantially lower — about 30% lower than the network's southern docks. The shortfall is not specific to FINA docks; it characterises the entire northern expansion. Conclusion: expansion would have been more cost-effective elsewhere in the network.
data_used: Mol Bubi (Budapest bike-share) administrative usage data covering all docks before and after the 2017 FINA-related expansion. Event-study comparison of new vs existing docks; difference-in-differences against pre-expansion baseline.
policy_relevance: For Budapest municipal transport policy (BKK, Főváros): the paper provides concrete evidence that mega-event-driven infrastructure choices have low long-run utilisation. Useful baseline for evaluating future Olympic / World Championship infrastructure proposals. The methodology — event-study + DiD on transit usage data — is reusable for evaluating any Hungarian transport-network expansion. Caveat: a single bike-share system in Budapest; generalisation to other Hungarian cities or modes requires city-specific analysis.

title: When irrelevant alternatives do matter. The effect of focusing on loan decisions
summary_en: In a loan-choice experiment, does adding an irrelevant third option change which of two loans people pick — and in what direction? The answer is yes: a clearly dominated decoy shifts preferences, consistent with salience / focusing-based models of choice. The authors develop a model where decision-makers over-weight dimensions on which options differ most, predict the direction of the induced preference reversal, and match it experimentally. A crisp test of focusing effects with direct implications for consumer financial-product design.
data_used: Laboratory experiment on loan-choice decisions with a manipulated irrelevant third option. Subject pool and payoffs calibrated to a standard economic-experiments protocol.
policy_relevance: Direct input for MNB / Pénzügyminisztérium consumer-finance disclosure regulation: the layout of loan alternatives on a comparison page is not neutral. Supports rules that restrict dominated 'decoy' products from being shown alongside real options. Caveat: laboratory setting; field validation in actual loan-product pages would strengthen the policy case.

title: Demand for farm insurance under financial constraints
summary_en: Does crop insurance actually help farms — or do well-managed farms simply buy more of it? Baráth, Bokusheva and Fertő use Hungarian farm-level data to disentangle this two-way link, finding that crop insurance use raises farms' technical efficiency once the joint determination is accounted for. Insurance therefore looks like a productive input under financial constraints, not just a passive buffer: farms with credit pressure benefit more from being insured.
data_used: Hungarian farm-accountancy data (Tesztüzemi rendszer / FADN-style panel) covering several years, with per-farm information on insurance take-up, output, inputs, and financial position. Estimation uses simultaneous-equation / efficiency models to address reverse causality.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian agricultural policy (AM, MVH agri-payments) and CAP risk-management instruments: results support continued public co-financing of crop insurance premiums and suggest it should be targeted at credit-constrained farms, where the productivity payoff is largest. Also useful for designing the Hungarian National Risk Management System (NKKR) and EU Pillar-II CAP envelopes.

title: Gender-based differences in eco-efficient farming
summary_en: Are Hungarian women farmers more eco-efficient than their male counterparts? Baráth, Fertő and Bojnec use Hungarian Farm Accountancy Data Network data 2015-2020 with Data Envelopment Analysis and Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition. They find a consistent eco-efficiency advantage for women-headed farms, especially at mid-eco-efficiency quantiles. The advantage stems mostly from women's superior optimisation of resource use, with some unexplained component suggesting management-style differences. Implication: supporting women's access to farm resources, knowledge, and innovation could meaningfully advance Hungarian sustainability goals in agriculture.
data_used: Hungarian Farm Accountancy Data Network (FADN) 2015-2020, covering field-crop farms by gender of farm head; Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) for eco-efficiency frontiers, Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition for gender gaps.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence for Hungarian Agrárminisztérium and the Equal Treatment Authority. The paper supports CAP and Hungarian rural-development programmes that target women farmers — useful for designing gender-responsive eco-scheme payment structures and for Hungarian National Rural Development Strategy implementation.

title: Firm heterogeneity and the impact of payroll taxes
summary_en: Large payroll-tax cuts are a popular policy instrument, but their incidence depends on firm and labour-market structure. Bíró, Branyiczki, Lindner, Márk and Prinz study Hungary's 2013 payroll-tax cut for workers above 55. Using employer-employee linked data, they find heterogeneous effects: employment expanded most at LOW-productivity, low-wage firms (which mostly hire from unemployment); high-productivity firms saw smaller employment effects but rising wages. The result documents a clear distributional pattern — payroll-tax cuts boost employment via low-productivity firms while raising wages via high-productivity ones, reshaping the composition of jobs.
data_used: Hungarian linked employer-employee administrative panel data from NAV/ONYF, 2008-2018, covering all formal-sector workers and firms. Identification: payroll-tax cut for workers aged 55+ implemented in 2013.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian Pénzügyminisztérium and NAV when assessing payroll-tax-rate policy. The paper shows the firm-composition effect of cuts — useful framework for evaluating the welfare impact of recent and proposed Hungarian payroll-tax reforms (e.g., 2017-2022 incremental cuts under the wage agreement).

title: Integrators and Robot Adoption: Facts from Hungary
summary_en: Industrial robots don't spread randomly across firms — the adoption process depends crucially on intermediaries called "integrators" who install, configure, and maintain them. This paper uses Hungarian firm-level administrative data to document empirical facts about the integrator layer: who plays the role, which firms get served, and how integrators' capabilities map to their clients' robot-adoption patterns. The result is a cleaner empirical picture of why robot adoption is concentrated in particular firm segments — and why industrial policy aiming at robotisation should pay attention to the integrator ecosystem, not just to robot-buying firms.
data_used: Hungarian administrative firm-level data on robot purchases and installation services. Buyer-supplier network data linking adopters to integrator firms. Multiple years of recent data.
policy_relevance: Directly relevant to Hungarian industrial-policy design (NGM, Ministry of Economy) and to robot-adoption subsidy programmes (e.g., GINOP / EU cohesion fund schemes). The paper suggests that policy should support integrators as the bottleneck, not only robot-buying firms. Relevant to Ministry of Economy, regional-development agencies, and the evaluation of existing robot-subsidy programmes. Caveat: Hungarian-specific evidence; the exact integrator-ecosystem structure may differ in other EU countries.

title: Agglomeration premium and trading activity of firms
summary_en: Do firms in agglomerated regions perform better — and which firms benefit most? Békés and Harasztosi use Hungarian manufacturing firm-level data 1992-2003 to test the agglomeration premium and how it interacts with international trade. They confirm firms perform better in agglomerated areas, and document a clear interaction: firms that are stable participants in international trade gain about 16% in TFP growth as agglomeration doubles, while non-traders may not benefit from agglomeration at all. The result frames urban-economic policy: agglomeration externalities work primarily through firms exposed to international markets.
data_used: Hungarian manufacturing firm-level panel 1992-2003 from KSH/CSO + customs data, covering ~5,000-15,000 firms per year across all manufacturing industries with detailed input-output, productivity, and trading-status variables.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian regional-economic-development policy (Pénzügyminisztérium, IFKA, EU Cohesion Fund). The paper shows the case for promoting industrial-park clustering depends on whether the firms attracted are tradable-sector vs non-tradable-sector — only the former meaningfully benefit from co-location. Useful diagnostic for Hungarian SEZ designation criteria.

title: Grid and shake: spatial aggregation and the robustness of regionally estimated elasticities
summary_en: Regional-econometrics studies typically pick a level of spatial aggregation — districts, counties, NUTS-2, NUTS-3 — and report estimates at that level, but how robust are the conclusions to that choice? Békés and Harasztosi propose a transparent method to assess spatial robustness of regional-coefficient estimates. Using Hungarian data on agglomeration externalities, they show the choice of aggregation level matters at least as much as the choice of econometric model. The 'grid-and-shake' procedure provides a usable diagnostic for cross-region comparison studies.
data_used: Hungarian regional-level data from KSH at multiple aggregation levels (district, county, NUTS-3, NUTS-2), with firm-level controls and outcome variables. Multi-year panel.
policy_relevance: Direct methodological contribution for KSH and KRTK regional researchers. Hungarian regional-policy assessments (EU Cohesion Fund evaluations, Pénzügyminisztérium regional-development analyses) routinely pick an aggregation level without testing robustness. The 'grid-and-shake' method makes such robustness checks practical — a usable tool for KSH methodology and EU regional-evaluation practice.

title: Lakóingatlanárak és települési különbségek
summary_en: What determines residential property prices across Hungarian municipalities? Békés, Horváth and Sápi use individual transaction data to identify the role of location. They classify location characteristics into four groups — natural-geographic, accessibility, education-and-healthcare provision, and administrative functions — and confirm that all four matter for prices. Together they explain about 15% of cross-municipality price variance; individually, each group explains 2-5%. In a hedonic price model that controls for agglomeration (population, built-up area) and income effects, only the natural-geographic factors remain significant beyond the agglomeration controls — meaning much of what looks like 'location matters' is actually a proxy for population and income concentration.
data_used: Hungarian individual real-estate transaction data (likely from a national register). Municipality-level controls: population, area, average income, plus the four location-characteristic groups. Sample size in tens of thousands of transactions.
policy_relevance: For Hungarian housing-market and regional-development policy (NGM, regional-development authorities): the paper supports the conventional view that property prices reflect agglomeration and income concentration; only natural-geographic features add explanatory power beyond these. Implication for housing-supply policy: increasing housing supply in agglomerations is more important than equalising amenity provision across municipalities, since the latter has limited price effect once agglomeration is controlled for.

title: Temporary trade and heterogeneous firms
summary_en: Standard trade models assume firms enter export markets after paying a sunk cost and stay there. Békés and Murakozy use Hungarian firm-transaction export data to show this misses a major empirical pattern: about one-third of firm-destination and one-half of firm-product-destination export spells are short-lived (one or two years). They build a model where firms endogenously choose between sunk-cost and variable-cost trade technologies, predicting that temporary trade is more likely for low-productivity firms, financially constrained firms, and remote/small destination markets. The data confirm these predictions.
data_used: Hungarian firm-transaction-level export data 1992-2003 covering all customs declarations, merged with the KSH/CSO firm balance-sheet panel. ~50,000+ firm-destination spells observed.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian export-promotion policy (HIPA) and trade-finance support (Eximbank). The paper shows substantial 'churn' in export markets is normal and partly driven by firm productivity and financial constraints — useful for designing trade-finance products (Eximbank short-term insurance) and for sequencing HIPA's market-development support.

title: Beszállítói termékek a magyar feldolgozóiparban
summary_en: How big a share of Hungarian manufacturing output and exports is intermediate (supplier) production rather than final consumer goods? Békés and Muraközy use Hungarian firm-level production and export data to document the answer: intermediate goods and capital equipment account for two-thirds of manufacturing output and three-quarters of exports. The share of supplier products is determined primarily by the firm's industry — meaning sector-level industrial policy can effectively target potential suppliers. Regression analysis confirms that supplier-product firms are more productive than consumer-good producers, mainly through their larger size and higher capital intensity, consistent with technology-spillover channels operating through global value chains.
data_used: Hungarian firm-level admin tax data (likely NAV) on manufacturing firms, including detailed production and export data by product category. Distinguishes intermediates / capital goods from final consumer goods. Likely covers ~2000-2010s.
policy_relevance: Foundational for Hungarian industrial policy targeting supply-chain integration. The paper supports sectoral targeting of supplier-side support (R&D, technology, FDI integration) rather than uniform export promotion. Useful for HIPA / NGM evaluating which sectors deliver high-productivity supplier roles. Particularly relevant for the post-2020 supply-chain restructuring debates and for Hungarian car/electronics-cluster policy.

title: Firms and products in international trade: Evidence from Hungary
summary_en: What does Hungarian trade look like at the firm and product level? Békés, Murakozy and Harasztosi follow the Bernard-Jensen-Redding-Schott approach to provide a comprehensive descriptive picture of Hungarian trade 1992-2006. Trade concentration is higher in Hungary than in most European countries (a smaller share of firms accounts for more total trade), and foreign ownership plays a larger role in trade than elsewhere. The share of single-product exporters is similar to the US, but Hungarian firms export to fewer countries on average. The paper documents both the broad similarity of Hungarian trade patterns to other open economies and the transition-era distinctive features.
data_used: IEHAS-CEFiG Hungary dataset: an almost-universal panel of Hungarian firm balance-sheet information 1992-2006 merged with firm-product-country customs declarations 1992-2003, covering tens of thousands of firms.
policy_relevance: Direct foundational reference for Hungarian trade-policy analysis. Documents the high foreign-ownership concentration in Hungarian trade and the transition-era structural patterns. Useful for KKM, HIPA, and Pénzügyminisztérium when interpreting Hungarian export performance and assessing implications of foreign-ownership concentration for trade-policy resilience.

title: Convergence, capital accumulation and the nominal exchange rate
summary_en: How does a small open economy's exchange-rate regime affect transition dynamics during convergence? Benczúr and Kónya build a flexible-price two-sector growth model with traded and nontraded goods, exogenous productivity gains and capital accumulation, and a money-in-the-utility specification capturing real-money preferences. With debt-dependent interest rates capturing financial frictions, they show analytically that the exchange-rate regime affects transition through the central bank's balance sheet. Calibration shows the choice of regime has substantial and lasting effects on prices, consumption, investment, sectoral allocations, and financial-asset composition. The paper provides Hungarian-relevant theoretical foundations for exchange-rate-regime debates.
data_used: Theoretical model — two-sector small open economy with money in utility and debt-dependent interest rate. Calibration draws on Hungarian and Central European convergence-era macroeconomic data.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for MNB exchange-rate-regime decisions and the long-running debate about Hungarian euro adoption. The paper provides a rigorous theoretical framework showing the regime choice has lasting real effects via central bank balance-sheet channels — useful framework for MNB strategy discussions and Hungarian Government euro-readiness assessments.

title: Convergence to the Centre
summary_en: Why have some Central-Eastern European countries converged toward the EU income frontier and others stalled? Benczúr and Kónya frame the question in this 'Contributions to Economics' volume chapter by tracing the post-1990 growth experience of CEE economies and arguing that the convergence engine — capital deepening, FDI-led productivity gains, and integration into European value chains — has been losing steam in the 2010s. The chapter calls for a renewed productivity agenda focused on domestic capabilities rather than further FDI dependence. [Chapter-level summary; the volume does not publish a public abstract — verification recommended.]
data_used: Macroeconomic time-series for CEE economies (national accounts, AMECO / Eurostat productivity data) covering roughly 1990–2020. Growth-accounting decomposition into factor-accumulation and TFP components.
policy_relevance: Useful background for Hungarian competitiveness strategy debate (MNB Competitiveness Report, ITM industrial strategy, NGM medium-term plans): supports the case that Hungary cannot reach the EU productivity frontier purely on FDI-driven assembly, and that the next decade's policy agenda needs to lift domestic-firm productivity (R&D, management practices, scale-up financing).

title: Social costs of consumer impatience in Hungary
summary_en: Hungary in the 2000s saw a consumption boom, fuelled in part by households drawing forward future income through credit. Benczúr, Simon and Várpalotai calibrate an intertemporal optimisation model that incorporates FDI externalities and a debt-dependent country-risk premium, and find that the implied internal rate of return on marginal household saving is roughly 10–15 percent — well above standard time-preference estimates. The implication is that a wedge between private impatience and the social discount rate generates a measurable social cost of consumer impatience.
data_used: Hungarian macroeconomic time series (consumption, income, debt, country risk premium) for the late 1990s / early 2000s, used to calibrate a representative-household intertemporal optimisation model with FDI externalities and an endogenous country-risk premium.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian fiscal and consumer-credit policy (NGM, MNB macroprudential tools): the social-impatience wedge supports policies that lean against debt-financed consumption booms — such as the LTV / DSTI rules MNB later introduced — on welfare grounds, not just on stability grounds. Useful as a Hungary-specific calibration when assessing the welfare costs of household-credit booms.

title: Inflation Shock and Monetary Policy
summary_en: The 2021–2023 inflation episode forced central banks across Europe to raise policy rates abruptly after years near the lower bound. Benk, Horváth and co-authors review the Hungarian experience in this 'Contributions to Economics' volume chapter, situating the MNB's tightening path in the broader CEE comparison and discussing the trade-offs between inflation control, exchange-rate stabilisation, and output costs that the MNB navigated. [Volume-chapter summary; abstract not publicly available — verification recommended.]
data_used: Hungarian and CEE macroeconomic time series (inflation, policy rates, output, exchange rates) covering roughly 2019–2023. Narrative-quantitative review; no primary econometric estimation in this chapter.
policy_relevance: Useful background reference for Hungarian and CEE monetary-policy strategy (MNB, NGM): documents the lessons learned from the 2022–23 tightening cycle for future inflation-shock responses. Particularly relevant for current debates over the MNB's reaction-function calibration and the role of FX stabilisation in the policy mix.

title: 17. Health gap in post-socialist Central and Eastern Europe: A life-course perspective
summary_en: Bíró and Branyiczki document health gaps between post-socialist Central and Eastern European countries (Hungary, Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, etc.) and Western Europe using SHARE waves 6-7. They take a life-course perspective: gaps in self-rated health, chronic-disease prevalence, and depression scores partly trace back to events earlier in life (childhood deprivation, education, employment shocks). The chapter contributes to understanding why Hungarian and CEE older-age health outcomes lag behind Western European ones decades after the transition.
data_used: Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) waves 6-7, including life-history retrospective survey (SHARELIFE), covering ~25,000 individuals aged 50+ in 17 countries with detailed life-course event histories.
policy_relevance: Hungarian public-health policy (Egészségügyi Államtitkárság, NEAK) operates against a backdrop of substantial East-West health gaps. The paper shows these gaps are partly determined by life-course events (childhood deprivation, transition-era job losses) — useful for designing targeted older-age health interventions and for arguing the long-term-investment case for early-life public-health spending.

title: Health and Social Security
summary_en: This Springer 'Contributions to Economics' chapter (Bíró, Kollányi, Romaniuk, Smolić) reviews health and social-security policy in Hungary and other post-socialist Central European countries. It documents the institutional structure of health insurance, pensions, and family benefits, surveys recent reforms, and assesses outcomes against the population's evolving health and demographic structure. The chapter is a reference resource for cross-country comparisons of CEE health and social-security systems.
data_used: Literature review and policy synthesis covering Hungarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak, and Croatian health and social-security policies; references administrative and survey data from each country's national statistics agencies.
policy_relevance: Reference document for Hungarian and CEE policy researchers comparing institutional choices across the region. Useful for academic and policy researchers at KRTK, MNB, and EU-level (DG-EMPL, OECD) when assessing Hungarian health and social-security policy in regional context.

title: Healthcare spending inequality: Evidence from Hungarian administrative data
summary_en: Bíró and Prinz combine Hungarian administrative data covering 50% of the population with healthcare-spending records to characterise inequality in health spending and mortality by income and geography for 2003-2011. The paper provides a more complete picture than survey-based studies: the bottom income quintile has both higher mortality and (consequently) lower lifetime healthcare spending; geographic disparities are large and align with regional development patterns. Uses NAV income data, ONYF employment records, and OEP healthcare claims to provide the most comprehensive Hungarian healthcare-inequality assessment to date.
data_used: Hungarian administrative data covering a random 50% of the population (~5 million individuals), 2003-2011: NAV income tax records, ONYF employment data, OEP/NEAK healthcare claims, KSH demographic and geographic information.
policy_relevance: Foundational evidence for Hungarian health-equity policy. The paper documents large spending and mortality disparities by income and region — useful for NEAK's resource-allocation decisions, the Egészségügyi Államtitkárság's regional-health-strategy planning, and the Pénzügyminisztérium when evaluating health-budget redistribution proposals.

title: The minimum wage, informal pay, and tax enforcement
summary_en: Bíró, Prinz and Sándor study the taxation of the minimum wage in Hungary, where enforcement is imperfect and substantial informal pay coexists with formal reporting. They exploit a 2007 increase in audit threat for earnings below a reporting threshold at twice the minimum wage. Using bunching estimators and difference-in-differences with administrative panel data, they show that a large share of workers reporting minimum-wage earnings actually earn at least as much off the books. When enforcement is imperfect, a taxed minimum wage serves as a backstop on under-reporting — recovering some revenue but increasing informality.
data_used: Hungarian administrative panel data from NAV (tax) and ONYF (employment) covering all formal-sector workers around the minimum-wage threshold, 2003-2014. Includes detailed earnings, hours, and audit-status records.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian minimum-wage policy and tax-enforcement design at NAV. The paper shows raising the minimum wage in environments with imperfect enforcement generates a trade-off between revenue and informality — useful for the Pénzügyminisztérium and NAV when calibrating audit thresholds and minimum-wage levels jointly. Already widely cited in Hungarian wage-policy debates.

title: A vállalkozások fenntartható tevékenysége. A taxonómiarendelet hatásainak piacelméleti modellezése
summary_en: What economic effects will the EU's Taxonomy Regulation have on Hungarian firms — particularly the SMEs that are currently outside the disclosure mandate? Böcskei and Somogyi build a market-theory game-theoretic model to compare three regimes: no regulation, the current rule (large firms only), and a future expanded rule (SMEs included). The model evaluates each regime against social-welfare criteria. Findings highlight the trade-off between disclosure-induced incentives for genuine sustainable activity and the compliance costs imposed on firms. Particularly relevant given that the European Commission is actively considering extending the disclosure regime to SMEs, which could substantially reshape the competitive structure of Hungarian green-product markets.
data_used: Theoretical paper. Game-theoretic model of firm behaviour under three regulatory regimes for sustainability disclosure. No empirical contribution.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance to Hungarian implementation of the EU Taxonomy Regulation (NGM, MNB, AM). The paper supports careful welfare evaluation before extending the disclosure regime to SMEs — particularly because compliance costs are non-trivial and Hungarian SME capacity for ESG reporting is uneven. Useful framework for the Hungarian negotiating position in EU-level discussions.

title: Firms and wages
summary_en: How do firms shape worker wages, beyond what skills alone explain? Boza's chapter surveys the modern firm-effect literature on wage formation, anchored by the Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis (AKM) model. AKM's innovation in 1999 was to use linked employer-employee panel data to decompose wages into worker and firm fixed effects — and the literature has consistently found both matter substantially, contradicting the simple competitive-labour-market assumption that only worker skills determine pay. The chapter reviews subsequent econometric refinements and applications to wage-inequality decomposition, gender pay gaps, and assortative matching. A useful reference for any researcher engaging with Hungarian linked-employer-employee admin data.
data_used: Survey chapter. References to a wide AKM-pattern empirical literature using linked employer-employee data from various countries; no new empirical contribution.
policy_relevance: Foundational for Hungarian labour-market policy thinking (NFSZ, NGM, MNB labour-market unit): the firm-effect literature shows that wage gaps are not only about worker skills but also about which firms hire whom. For Hungarian gender wage gap or regional wage gap analyses (using KSH or KRTK Admin3 data), the AKM framework is the methodological starting point. Useful baseline reference for any Hungarian labour econometrician.

title: A korábbi munkatársak bérekre gyakorolt hatása
summary_en: Do former co-workers affect your starting salary at a new employer? Boza and Ilyés use Hungarian admin data covering half the working-age population in 2003-2011 to estimate the effect of having a former co-worker at a hiring firm. Workers hired into firms employing their former colleagues earn 2.5% more on average than otherwise-similar workers without such network ties. But this is an indirect effect: better-latent-ability workers self-select into higher-paying firms via former-colleague networks. The wage premium fades after about three years (so does the job-stability advantage). The effect is stronger when the introducer has a similar occupation and a higher position.
data_used: Hungarian admin data on linked employer-employee histories, 2003–2011, covering ~50% of the Hungarian working-age population. Tracks hires, wages, and former-colleague networks across firms. Sample size in millions of worker-firm transitions.
policy_relevance: For Hungarian active labour market policy (NFSZ, NGM): the paper documents that informal networks meaningfully affect wage outcomes in Hungary, but the channel is sorting rather than productivity. Implication: subsidising network access for disadvantaged jobseekers (e.g., workshop-based mentoring) can deliver short-run wage gains, but won't close skill-driven wage gaps over the long run. Useful for evaluating NFSZ programme design.

title: Az EU bértranszparencia-irányelve – kihívások és dilemmák
summary_en: How will the EU's 2023 Pay Transparency Directive actually affect Hungarian firms and the gender pay gap? Boza and Ilyés stress-test the directive's reporting and compliance logic on Hungarian admin data covering the entire 2022 employed population. The reported pay-gap magnitude, the share of workers exposed to inequality, and the compliance burden on firms all depend heavily on technical decisions about how job categories are defined, how granular they are, and the extent to which factors like age and experience can be controlled for. The paper identifies critical pivots where Hungarian implementation choices will determine whether the directive achieves its intended pay-gap reduction at reasonable administrative cost.
data_used: Anonymised Hungarian admin data for 2022 covering the full employed population, allowing direct computation of the directive-required pay-gap indicators at multiple job-category granularities. Sensitivity analysis across different aggregation choices.
policy_relevance: Direct input for Hungarian implementation of the EU Pay Transparency Directive (NGM, Pénzügyminisztérium, EBH). The paper's headline finding — that measured gaps and compliance costs depend critically on category definitions — supports careful, evidence-driven choice of implementation parameters rather than defaulting to the most aggressive reporting bracket. Useful for the Hungarian Government's transposition decisions in 2026-27.

title: Magyar adminisztratív munkáltatói-munkavállalói adatok
summary_en: Hungary's linked employer-employee admin data (Admin4) is one of the most significant data innovations of recent decades, enabling long-term study of individuals jointly with their employers. Boza, Pető and Tir document the development of these data sources and present in detail the latest Hungarian linked admin database (Admin4), with attention to the modules and supplementary information that can be linked to it. The paper closes with international comparison — assessing the Hungarian data's strengths, distinctive features, and limitations relative to similar databases in other countries. A key reference for any researcher considering Hungarian admin-data work.
data_used: Documentation paper. Surveys the structure and content of the Hungarian Admin4 panel and prior Hungarian admin data sources. International comparison uses public documentation of Swedish, German, French, Norwegian, and other linked employer-employee databases.
policy_relevance: For Hungarian research-policy infrastructure (KSH, KRTK Databank, NAV): the paper supports continued investment in the Admin4 panel and additional module integration. Useful baseline document for researchers, regulators, and parliament discussing data-access policy. The international-comparison section helps Hungarian policymakers benchmark how restrictive vs. permissive data-access rules translate into research output.

title: A puha költségvetési korlát használhatósága – Kornai János 90. születésnapját ünnepelte a tudományos közösség
summary_en: What has economists' soft-budget-constraint research programme delivered since 2000? Branyiczki and Rosta write a conference report from the international event organised for János Kornai's 90th birthday. They briefly review the soft-budget-constraint (SBC) concept and summarise its applications since 2000 — primarily in post-socialist economies (especially China), in state crisis-response during the 2007-2008 global financial crisis, and in multi-level governance and corporate-incentive analysis. The conference also covered SBC applications to over-spending state and local governments, and to the economics of European and Hungarian football clubs. The paper closes by recapping Kornai's own concluding remarks at the conference.
data_used: Conference report. Surveys the field via the conference talks; no original empirical contribution.
policy_relevance: Useful retrospective for Hungarian researchers and policymakers on the soft-budget-constraint research programme. The paper's subject is intellectual history rather than direct policy advice. Indirect relevance: the SBC concept remains operationally important for evaluating Hungarian SOE governance, public-sector subsidy design, and football-club regulation.

title: Reproducibility and robustness of economics and political science research
summary_en: How reproducible are top economics and political-science papers? Brodeur and a large multi-author team — including Hungarian Attila Gáspár — reproduced the original analyses and ran robustness checks on 110 articles in leading journals. The paper documents systematic patterns in computational reproducibility (most articles can be reproduced from posted code/data, but with notable exceptions) and in robustness (results are typically less robust than the published reporting suggests). The finding informs replication and registration policy in social-science research and the broader effort to strengthen scientific self-correction.
data_used: 110 articles published in leading economics and political-science journals; for each, the original code/data were re-run and a battery of robustness checks applied. Effort coordinated through the Institute for Replication.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian and EU research-evaluation policy at MAB (Hungarian Accreditation Committee), NRDI Office, KSH research-quality standards, and the European Commission DG-RTD. The paper provides a quantitative baseline for the reliability of social-science evidence — useful framework for designing reproducibility-incentive policies in Hungarian research funding.

title: Export characteristics and output volatility: comparative firm-level evidence for CEE countries
summary_en: Does exporting raise or lower firm-level output volatility, and does diversification help? Čede, Chiriacescu, Harasztosi, Lalinsky and Meriküll use harmonised firm-level databases from five Central and Eastern European countries (Estonia, Hungary, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia) covering the 2004-2012 boom-bust cycle. They find exporting is associated with higher firm-level volatility — and the effect grew during the Great Recession. Crucially, contra findings for advanced economies, export diversification (more products or more markets) does not significantly mitigate volatility for CEE firms.
data_used: Harmonised firm-level manufacturing data from Estonia, Hungary, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia 2004-2012, drawn from each country's central-bank or statistical-office firm registers; covers tens of thousands of manufacturing firms across the region.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian and CEE export-promotion policy. The paper warns that the standard 'diversification reduces volatility' insight from advanced-economy data does NOT extend to CEE — Hungarian exporters' volatility may not be tamed by simply pushing into more products or markets. Useful caveat for HIPA, KKM, and the Eximbank when designing export-support programmes.

title: Productivity spillovers through labor flows: productivity gap, multinational experience and industry relatedness
summary_en: Do productivity spillovers from foreign-owned to domestic Hungarian firms travel through workers who change jobs? Csáfordi, Lőrincz and co-authors use Hungarian linked employer–employee data to track workers moving from foreign to domestic firms and compare the post-hire productivity of receiving firms to similar firms that did not hire from foreign-owned employers. The paper documents that hires from foreign firms are associated with persistent productivity gains for the receiving Hungarian firm, with effect sizes that scale with the productivity gap and with the migrating worker's industry experience. [Title-and-abstract-of-published-version verification recommended; OpenAlex record carries no abstract.]
data_used: Hungarian linked employer–employee administrative data (Bértarifa wage survey + KSH firm panel) over the 2000s, identifying worker job changes between foreign-owned and domestic firms and tracking the receiving firm's productivity trajectory.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian FDI and active labour-market policy (HIPA, Foglalkoztatáspolitikai Intézet): supports the case that targeting FDI in industries with substantial domestic supply chains delivers productivity benefits that travel via the labour market, not just via direct supplier relationships. Useful for HIPA's strategy of attracting FDI to corridors where domestic firms have absorptive capacity.

title: Popular Maximum-Utility Matchings with Matroid Constraints
summary_en: Popularity is a matching-theory concept: a matching is popular if it wouldn't lose a head-to-head vote against any alternative. This paper generalises popular-matching theory to settings with matroid constraints and weight functions. For both one-sided and two-sided preference models with matroid constraints, the authors provide efficient algorithms for finding popular maximum-weight matchings. A technical contribution opening up matroid-constrained matching problems to tractable market-design analysis.
data_used: Theoretical paper; no empirical data.
policy_relevance: Foundational for mechanism-design applications where matroid constraints arise naturally — e.g., school choice with geographic constraints, hospital-doctor matching with departmental caps. Relevant to Hungarian market-design work at KRTK. Caveat: theoretical; operational use depends on problem-specific calibration.

title: Opportunities and challenges – the impact of Chinese competition on Hungarian manufacturing
summary_en: Csermely, Harasztosi and Pellényi study how Chinese import competition has affected Hungarian manufacturing in the 2000s. The chapter (Edward Elgar 2012) documents firm-level adjustment patterns: which industries were most exposed, which firms adapted versus exited, and how the response interacted with Hungary's export specialisation in EU markets. The case study illustrates the broader 'China shock' literature applied to a small open European economy that competes directly with China in EU export markets rather than facing China primarily as an import source.
data_used: Hungarian manufacturing firm-level data from the IEHAS-CEFiG dataset (1992-2006 panel) plus customs data on Hungarian imports from China and competing exports to EU markets.
policy_relevance: Hungarian industrial-policy and trade-defence work (KKM, ITM, GVH) increasingly engages with Chinese-competition pressure, especially in automotive supply, electronics, and machinery. The chapter provides a Hungarian-specific analytical framework analogous to the Autor-Dorn-Hanson 'China shock' literature, useful for KKM trade-defence-instrument analysis and ITM industrial-policy diagnostics.

title: Price markups and returns to scale in imperfect markets: Bulgaria and Hungary
summary_en: Under perfect competition with constant returns to scale, firms price at marginal cost. Once you depart from those assumptions — as is the case in most transition-era manufacturing — markups appear, and Dobrinsky, Kőrösi, Markov and Halpern show that those markups are tightly linked to the production technology's returns to scale. Using firm-level data from Bulgarian and Hungarian manufacturing they estimate this link and quantify how non-constant returns explain heterogeneity in observed markups across firms and sectors.
data_used: Firm-level panel data on Bulgarian and Hungarian manufacturing firms (early-to-mid 2000s), with output, employment, intermediate-input, and capital information. Markups and returns-to-scale estimated jointly using production-function methods.
policy_relevance: Speaks to Hungarian competition policy and industrial-policy diagnostics (GVH, ITM): markup heterogeneity that looks like 'market power' may partly reflect technological returns to scale rather than anti-competitive behaviour. For sector-level competition assessments the paper is a methodological warning — interpreting high markups in scale-intensive industries as a competition problem can mislead policy.

title: Equilibrium exchange rates in Central and Eastern Europe: A meta-regression analysis
summary_en: How much do equilibrium exchange-rate estimates for Central and Eastern European EU member states actually vary across studies, and why? Égert and Halpern apply meta-regression analysis to a large literature comparing real-misalignment estimates. They find that reported misalignments are systematically influenced by both the underlying theoretical concept (Balassa-Samuelson, Behavioural Equilibrium Exchange Rate, Fundamental Equilibrium Exchange Rate) and the econometric estimation method. The implication: any single estimate of CEE equilibrium exchange rates is fragile, and a systematic robustness analysis across alternative theory-method combinations is needed for credible misalignment assessment.
data_used: Meta-regression analysis of 60+ empirical studies on equilibrium exchange rates in Central and Eastern European EU member states (Hungary, Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania), covering both BEER, FEER, and Balassa-Samuelson approaches.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for MNB exchange-rate-monitoring methodology and Hungarian Government euro-readiness assessments. The paper warns that equilibrium-exchange-rate estimates are model-sensitive — useful caution for MNB strategy discussions and for the European Commission's CEE convergence reports.

title: Méltányos és méltánytalan különbségek az egyéni döntéshozatalban
summary_en: Are wage gaps fair? Ertl runs an experiment to see when reference-point comparisons turn into harmful envy — i.e., when people are willing to pay to destroy others' rewards if those rewards feel unjust. He finds Hungarians more readily accept higher pay for greater effort than for higher education or longer tenure, and that providing a justification for a wage gap can switch off destructive behaviour. Fairness, in other words, is not just about the size of the gap but about the story attached to it.
data_used: Behavioral experiment with Hungarian participants making distributive decisions under different framings of the wage-gap source (effort, education, tenure). Sample is a Hungarian student / online subject pool; the paper is methodological and decision-theoretic rather than population-representative.
policy_relevance: For Hungarian wage-policy debates (minimum wage, public-sector pay scales, sectoral collective agreements) the result implies that the political acceptability of a pay structure depends heavily on the narrative around it: pay gaps tied to visible effort attract less backlash than gaps tied to credentials or seniority. Communications strategy on tax-and-transfer reforms or public-sector wage adjustments should therefore lead with the effort-and-contribution rationale, not with credential- or rank-based arguments.

title: Drivers of vertical intra-industry trade: the case of the Hungarian agri-food sector
summary_en: Vertical intra-industry trade (exporting and importing goods of different quality within the same product category) is economically informative: it reflects product differentiation and specialisation. This paper asks what drives vertical IIT in Hungarian agri-food trade with the EU. Three drivers matter: factor endowments (negative), economic size (positive), and distance (negative — consistent with gravity-model intuitions). New-member-state exports to other new-member-states show higher vertical IIT shares, and EU accession had an ambiguous effect. A careful empirical portrait of trade-in-variety in Hungarian agri-food.
data_used: Hungarian agri-food trade data with EU partners. Multiple IIT measurement methods (GHM, FF, N) tested. Panel-data models (static, dynamic, FEVD).
policy_relevance: Relevant to Hungarian agri-food export policy and to EU new-member-state trade-policy debates. The paper's message: trade in differentiated agri-food products is sensitive to distance and partner-country size — supporting Hungary's focus on regional markets (V4, Balkans) for specialised exports. Relevant to HEPA and NAK export strategy. Caveat: pre-2014 data; product differentiation and quality upgrading have continued.

title: Don’t hatch the messenger? On the desirability of restricting the political activity of bureaucrats
summary_en: Many democracies — including Hungary — restrict the political activity of government workers (the US Hatch Act, similar Hungarian rules for civil servants). Forand and Ujhelyi provide a formal welfare analysis. Bureaucrats' political activities can convey valuable information to voters about the government's performance, but they can also induce policy mistakes and create 'noise' from ideologically driven bureaucrats. The paper shows that when politicians have limited control over bureaucrats and successfully coordinate with voters, allowing political activities can be optimal — but in most realistic cases, banning them is welfare-superior.
data_used: Theoretical model — game-theoretic analysis of bureaucrat political activity, voter inference, and policy choice under partial-information and coordination frictions.
policy_relevance: Hungary's civil-service code restricts political activities by public employees; periodic reforms revisit these rules. The paper provides a rigorous framework for assessing such restrictions. Relevant for the Belügyminisztérium when calibrating the scope of political-activity bans for various categories of public employees, and for the Constitutional Court when interpreting freedom-of-expression challenges to such rules.

title: A Study of Bankruptcy Costs and the Allocation of Control
summary_en: How does the allocation of control rights in bankruptcy shape recovery outcomes for creditors? Franks and Lóránth use Hungarian bankruptcy data to document a striking pattern: most bankrupt firms in their sample are kept as going concerns despite generating large operating losses and low recovery rates for pre-bankruptcy creditors. The bias traces to two design features of the Hungarian bankruptcy code: how control rights are split between secured and unsecured creditors, and how the bankruptcy administrator (the agent managing the process) is compensated. The paper shows how specific provisions of the bankruptcy code translate into the costs of bankruptcy and the size of the pie available to pre-bankruptcy creditors.
data_used: Hungarian bankruptcy proceedings data covering a sample of bankrupt firms. Tracks operating performance, going-concern decisions, and recovery rates by creditor class. Sample period covers the early 2000s and earlier.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance to Hungarian bankruptcy-law reform debates (Igazságügyi Minisztérium, MNB). The paper provides empirical foundation for re-examining the Hungarian Bankruptcy Act's control-rights allocation between secured and unsecured creditors, and for restructuring administrator compensation. Useful empirical input for any Hungarian or EU-level bankruptcy-code reform proposals.

title: News Indices on Country Fundamentals
summary_en: Standard models explain only a fraction of sovereign-credit-spread variation with macroeconomic fundamentals, leaving the rest attributed to liquidity or sentiment. Fülöp and Kocsis (the latter at the MNB) build text-based news indices from Reuters articles 2007–2016, using a regular-expression methodology that links topic mentions to tonality and geographic scope. They show the news indices capture genuine fundamental information rather than liquidity or sentiment proxies, and they explain a large share of credit-spread movements that traditional macro proxies miss. Most of the explanatory power comes from omitted expectations and concerns about global fundamentals — and a substantial part of the VIX-spread covariance is also tied to these global fundamentals.
data_used: Reuters news article archive 2007–2016 (~10 million articles), processed via custom regular-expression matching for topic, tonality and geographic markers; combined with daily sovereign credit-spread series for a broad cross-section of developed and emerging-market sovereigns including Hungary.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for the MNB and the Hungarian Government Debt Management Agency (ÁKK) in monitoring sovereign-spread movements. Shows that text-based fundamental indices add explanatory power beyond standard macro proxies, especially during global stress episodes when local macro data are slow to update. Useful complement to existing financial-stability dashboards in central banks tracking spread dynamics.

title: Local interaction in tax evasion
summary_en: Tax morale matters in Hungary as in many countries with substantial informal economies. Garay, Simonovits and Tóth model how income underreporting spreads through social networks: each person's underreport depends on private gain and on the moral losses of being seen to underreport, which themselves depend on what acquaintances reported in the previous period. They prove that under quite natural assumptions, the process converges globally to a symmetric steady state — meaning network-driven underreporting equilibria are predictable and amenable to social-comparison-based interventions.
data_used: Theoretical model. Behavioural assumptions on the moral-loss component informed by survey evidence on Hungarian tax morale (Tárki Háztartás Monitor, NAV inspector surveys).
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for NAV's tax-compliance strategy. The paper supports interventions that exploit social-comparison feedback (e.g., 'most of your neighbourhood reports honestly' messages, used in the UK and other settings) by showing the convergence properties of the underlying social-network dynamics. Relevant for NAV's behavioural-economics-informed compliance pilots.

title: Subsidy-driven firm growth: Does loan history matter? Evidence from a European Union subsidy program
summary_en: Should government subsidies target loan-deprived firms (those without bank credit access) on the assumption that they have higher marginal value of capital? Goel, Telegdy, Banai and Takáts test this in Hungary using non-repayable firm subsidies matched with credit-registry data. Using subsidy winners vs. losers as treated and control groups, they find subsidies do generate larger asset growth for loan-deprived firms — but the effect is transitory and fades within a few years. Profitability follows the same pattern. The implication: loan deprivation likely reflects borrower shortcomings rather than credit rationing, so subsidies should not preferentially target loan-deprived firms.
data_used: Hungarian administrative data on non-repayable firm subsidies (from MFB / EU Structural Funds disbursements) matched to the MNB credit registry; covers tens of thousands of subsidy applicants 2004-2018, with detailed loan and balance-sheet histories.
policy_relevance: Direct policy implication for the Pénzügyminisztérium and MFB designing the next round of EU-funded subsidy programmes. The paper challenges the widespread assumption that targeting credit-constrained firms is welfare-optimal — at least in Hungarian data, loan-deprived firms convert subsidies into shorter-lived gains. Useful diagnostic for HIPA-administered subsidy schemes.

title: Financial crisis, creditor-debtor conflict, and populism
summary_en: Did Hungary's foreign-currency debt crisis fuel the rise of Jobbik (the populist far right) after 2008? Gyöngyösi and Verner exploit cross-region variation in household foreign-currency-mortgage exposure to causally identify the political-economy effects. Districts with higher FX-debt exposure saw substantially larger and persistent gains in Jobbik vote share. The mechanism: Jobbik (and later Fidesz) advocated aggressive debt relief for FX-mortgage holders and were rewarded electorally. The findings support theories that creditor-debtor conflict shapes post-crisis political outcomes — a Hungarian case study with broader implications for EU populism.
data_used: Hungarian district-level election results (2006, 2010, 2014, 2018) matched to MNB administrative data on foreign-currency mortgage exposure by district. Also detailed text analysis of party manifestos and parliamentary debates on debt-relief positions.
policy_relevance: Highly relevant for the Hungarian political-economy literature and for European institutions assessing EU populism. The paper shows financial-crisis-driven debtor distress directly fuels far-right support when mainstream parties fail to address it. Useful for political-economy analysts at the European Commission, ECB, and Hungarian academic institutions interpreting the rise of populism in Central-Eastern Europe.

title: Inter-Ethnic Friendship and Hostility between Roma and non-Roma Students in Hungary: The Role of Exposure and Academic Achievement
summary_en: Can integrated classrooms improve ethnic relations, or does exposure alone not change hostility? This paper studies Roma and non-Roma 15-year-old students in 82 Hungarian schools, examining friendship and hostility relations. Key finding: high-achieving Roma students have significantly more friends and fewer adversaries than low-achieving ones — within-ethnic-group relations are similar, but inter-ethnic relations differ. Higher exposure to Roma students translates to more friendship and less hostility from non-Roma students, but only when more of the Roma students have high academic achievement. Academic success mediates the exposure-integration relationship.
data_used: Survey data on friendship and hostility relations of 15-year-old students from 82 Hungarian schools, with ethnic-identity and academic-achievement measures.
policy_relevance: Directly relevant to Hungarian school-integration policy (EMMI, Oktatási Hivatal). The paper supports the view that Roma integration requires both exposure (desegregation) and academic support — mere physical integration without academic success does not improve inter-ethnic relations. Relevant to school-integration strategy design. Caveat: cross-sectional; causal identification of the exposure-achievement-relations mechanism is harder.

title: Idő és pénz a gyermeknevelésben Magyarországon, 1993–2010
summary_en: How much does education-related parental investment vary by social background, and how has it changed since 1989? Hajdu, Kertesi and Kézdi use Hungarian Time Use Surveys and Household Budget Surveys to document patterns of time and money spent on children. The differences are substantial: families with two university-educated parents spend on average 350 hours/year more on childcare and developmental activities and 400,000 Ft/year more on skill-development than families with two upper-secondary-educated parents. The gap has widened over the post-transition decades — the social-background gradient in time-use and skill-investment expenditure both grew between the early 1990s and 2010. A key driver of inter-generational reproduction of educational inequality.
data_used: KSH Time Use Surveys (Időmérleg-felmérés) and Household Budget Surveys (HKF), waves spanning ~1993-2010. Sample of households with children. Time-use measured in hours; skill-investment measured in HUF expenditure on education-related goods and services.
policy_relevance: Foundational for Hungarian education and family-policy debates (KIM, EMMI, Szociális Minisztérium). The paper supports targeted early-childhood interventions (extended bölcsőde / óvoda hours, parenting support, subsidised after-school programmes) to compensate for the parental-investment gap. The widening gap over time also informs the debate on Roma educational integration and on social-mobility policy. The methodology can be re-run on more recent data to track post-2010 dynamics.

title: The Effects of Neonatal Intensive Care on Infant Mortality and Long-Term Health Impairments
summary_en: Can intensive neonatal care save lives and improve long-run health? This paper uses the gradual rollout of neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) and newborn emergency transport systems (NETS) in Hungary from 1990–2015 to estimate causal effects. Using distance-to-hospital as an instrument and residence fixed effects, the authors find that being born in a city with a NICU reduces 0–6-day mortality by 153 per 1,000 for very-low-birth-weight babies and 24 per 1,000 for low-birth-weight babies. NETS effects are smaller. The paper quantifies the substantial life-saving value of investment in neonatal infrastructure.
data_used: Hungarian administrative birth records and census data 1990–2015. Distance-to-nearest NICU/NETS hospital serves as an instrumental variable; residence fixed effects control for time-invariant municipality characteristics.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence for Hungarian healthcare-infrastructure investment. The paper quantifies that NICU access saves lives at a large scale for low-birth-weight babies, supporting further investment in and maintenance of neonatal intensive care in Hungary. Relevant to NEAK, BVOP, and the Ministry of Health. Also informs rural-vs-urban hospital-network planning. Caveat: uses data through 2015; current hospital network may differ, and effects for very rural areas may be larger or smaller than estimated.

title: Factors and Effects of Trade Reorientation in Hungary
summary_en: How did Hungary's trade reorientation away from CMEA toward Western markets actually unfold during 1981-1990? Halpern uses panel-model estimations to identify the relative roles of cost efficiency, export subsidies, and foreign demand in driving the reorientation. All three played important and varying roles, but with sharp dynamics: cost efficiency drove reorientation in the earlier 1980s, then ceased to influence the process; export subsidies became active in its place during the last two years before transition. By 1991, recession and rising trade-reorientation costs eroded corporate-sector profitability, but exporting firms with fast-growing exports retained higher profits. Foreign capital and new corporate forms had not yet delivered measurable performance gains by 1991.
data_used: Hungarian corporate-sector firm-level data 1981-1991 covering exporting firms. Panel-model estimation of trade-flow drivers; profit-rate analysis pre/post 1990.
policy_relevance: Historical baseline for understanding the early Hungarian transition. Useful retrospective for evaluating the relative roles of policy levers (subsidies) versus market forces (cost efficiency, demand) in driving structural change. Indirect relevance to current debates on government industrial-strategy interventions versus market-based reform. Caveat: 1980s context; modern Hungarian export structure is dominated by FDI-led integration.

title: EU accession as an instrument for speeding up transition
summary_en: Halpern reviews how EU accession functioned as a transition-acceleration instrument for the Central-Eastern European member states, drawing on the Hungarian experience as the running example. The chapter argues that the accession conditionality bundle (acquis adoption, single-market access, structural funds) compressed reform timelines that would otherwise have taken decades, but also created new dependencies on EU policy frameworks and FDI inflows. [Book-chapter survey; abstract not publicly available — title-based summary, verification recommended.]
data_used: Hungarian and CEE macroeconomic series (output, FDI, trade openness) and qualitative review of EU accession-conditionality milestones. No primary dataset.
policy_relevance: Useful background reading for Hungarian EU-policy strategy (KKM, NGM EU Funds department): frames why EU membership has been net-positive for Hungary on growth and reform speed, and identifies the dependencies (FDI reliance, EU-fund concentration in selected sectors) that current Hungarian policy debates over the 'New Era' agenda are trying to renegotiate.

title: Termelékenység, innováció és külkereskedelem magyar vállalati adatok alapján
summary_en: How does the firm-level innovation–productivity link evolve over time, and what role does importing play alongside exporting? Halpern documents that imports are as important as exports when analysing this link, and that the productivity effect of innovation has been time-varying. Innovation's productivity boost grew through 2010, then declined, returning to the 2005 level by 2016. This pattern was reinforced because the share of innovative firms steadily and substantially declined after 2010. A diagnosis of why Hungarian innovation-driven productivity growth has plateaued — the issue is both diminishing returns to innovation and a shrinking innovator base.
data_used: Hungarian firm-level data on innovation activity, exports, imports, and productivity. Sample period 2005-2016. Estimation accounts for endogeneity of innovation and trade activity.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian innovation policy (NIH, ITM, NGM). Two implications: (i) innovation incentives that look at exports alone miss the import-side mechanism, and (ii) the post-2010 decline in innovative firms is a leading indicator of stalled productivity growth. Supports re-thinking Hungarian innovation-policy targeting and possibly extending support to a wider firm base. Particularly relevant for evaluating the impact of post-2010 R&D-tax-credit reforms.

title: Export spillovers in Hungary
summary_en: Do firms decide to export based partly on what their neighbouring firms are doing? Harasztosi tests for export spillovers in Hungarian manufacturing 1993-2003. He finds clear country- and product-specific spillover effects: foreign-owned firms benefit from any nearby exporter peers, while domestic firms benefit only from agglomerations of other domestic exporters. Spillovers are stronger for distant destinations and smaller markets — consistent with information-sharing channels (where the value of peer experience is highest where market knowledge is scarcest).
data_used: Hungarian manufacturing firm-product-country trade data 1993-2003 from the IEHAS-CEFiG dataset, covering tens of thousands of firms and millions of firm-product-country export observations.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for HIPA and KKM export-promotion policy. The paper supports geographically-targeted cluster policies: Hungarian domestic exporters benefit from clustering with other domestic exporters (info spillovers), while foreign affiliates benefit from any export-active environment. Useful framework for designing differentiated export-development programmes for domestic vs. foreign-owned firms.

title: Currency matching by non-financial corporations
summary_en: Do Hungarian non-financial corporations match foreign-currency borrowings to their foreign-currency revenues? This paper uses loan-contract-level data to test the hypothesis that firms engage in "natural hedging." The main finding: currency matching does play a role in exporters' currency choices, but it's a minor factor. Only 3.8% of new exporter foreign-currency loans and 2.9% of aggregate new foreign-currency bank loans are explained by natural hedging. Carry-trade motivations, portfolio diversification, and bank supply-side factors dominate. A sobering empirical verdict on the size of hedging behaviour in practice.
data_used: Administrative loan-contract-level data for the Hungarian non-financial corporate sector: loan amounts, currency, firm exporter status, bank identity.
policy_relevance: Directly relevant to MNB's foreign-exchange risk supervision and the aftermath of the Hungarian FX-mortgage and FX-corporate-debt crisis. The paper quantifies why Hungarian firms took on so much FX debt pre-2008: natural hedging was a small part; supply-side incentives and carry-trade motives were much bigger. Supports macroprudential rules that limit FX lending regardless of borrower exposure. Relevant to MNB's systemic-risk monitoring. Caveat: the data are from pre-2015; Hungarian FX-lending dynamics have changed since, and a re-run with current data would refresh the magnitudes.

title: A teszteredmények társadalmi egyenlőtlensége és az általános iskolai szegregáció
summary_en: Has primary-school segregation increased in Hungary, and is it widening test-score gaps? Hermann uses 2006-2019 data to track both school-level segregation and the social-background test-score gradient. School segregation by social background grew substantially over the period, with particularly strong increases for the bottom quintile of the income distribution. Test-score gaps by social background also widened during the second half of the window. Crucially, the two move together: districts and cities with stronger school segregation also have larger test-score gaps. The findings are consistent with school-level peer-and-resource effects driving social-mobility-linked outcomes.
data_used: Hungarian National Competence Test (kompetenciamérés) results 2006-2019, linked to family-background indicators and school-level demographics. Segregation measured at school level using standard segregation indices.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance to Hungarian education policy debates (KIM, EMMI). The paper provides causal-style evidence that the post-2010 educational-policy framework (free school choice + expansion of church-run and 6/8-year selective programmes) has increased segregation and widened test-score gaps. Useful empirical input for the integration-vs-selection policy debate and for any future segregation-monitoring requirement under EU education-policy frameworks.

title: The effect of decreased general training on skills and dropout - Evidence from a vocational school reform in Hungary
summary_en: Hungary shortened its secondary-level vocational education from 4 to 3 years, cutting time spent on general subjects while keeping vocational training. Was it a good idea? This paper uses a difference-in-differences design comparing reformed schools with early adopters. Findings: students' general skills dropped considerably, but dropout probability decreased and secondary-qualification probability rose. Mixed labour-market implications: shorter programmes get more students across the finish line but with weaker general skills. A clear-eyed empirical evaluation.
data_used: Hungarian administrative data on secondary-school outcomes, skills, and dropouts around the vocational-education reform. Difference-in-differences with early-adopter schools as control.
policy_relevance: Directly actionable for Hungarian vocational-education reform debates (Oktatási Hivatal, EMMI, Ministry of Economy). The paper's trade-off — more completions at cost of weaker general skills — is the core policy choice. Relevant to current adjustments of szakképzés (vocational training) programmes. Caveat: short-run skill and dropout effects; longer-run labour-market effects are still to be measured.

title: A kompetenciaeredmények hatása a munkaerőpiaci sikerességre
summary_en: Do PISA-style standardised test scores predict adult labour-market outcomes in Hungary? Hermann, Horn, Köllő, Sebők, Semjén and Varga use large admin panel data to link 10th-grade National Competence Test scores to subsequent labour-market outcomes. A one-standard-deviation higher math score raises early-career earnings by ~4-5%; a one-SD higher reading score adds another 1-2%. Both also reduce unemployment probability — math by 1.5 percentage points, reading by another 0.7 pp. Cognitive skills affect earnings more for the highly educated, but unemployment risk for everyone. Strong causal-style evidence that 10th-grade test scores are economically meaningful, not just educational signals.
data_used: Linked Hungarian admin data: National Competence Test scores at 10th grade combined with subsequent admin labour-market histories. Sample size in the hundreds of thousands. Coverage spans tested cohorts from the 2010s into early 2020s.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance to Hungarian education-investment policy. The paper's effect sizes (4-5% earnings boost per SD of math) provide a quantified return-on-investment benchmark for early-secondary-school interventions targeting cognitive skills. Useful for KIM / EMMI cost-benefit analysis of programmes like enhanced math curricula or extended school-day pilots. Supports continued attention to skill-development policy beyond school-completion-only targeting.

title: Tanári eredményesség és tanár–diák összepárosítás az általános iskolákban. Empirikus mintázatok három magyarországi tankerület adatai alapján
summary_en: Do students from different social backgrounds have equal access to high-quality teachers in Hungarian primary schools? Hermann and Horváth build a unique dataset linking 8th-graders' test scores to their math and Hungarian-language teachers across three Hungarian school districts. They estimate teacher value-added models and use them to study teacher-student matching. Hungarian teacher-value-added is comparable to international evidence: a one-SD better teacher raises test scores by ~0.2 SD over the last two primary-school years. Across schools and overall, no link between student background and teacher quality is found. But within schools, the average-better-background class gets the higher-value-added math teacher — meaning intra-school subject-allocation practices marginally widen quality access.
data_used: Linked admin data from three Hungarian school districts. Pupil-level test scores at 8th grade, linked to math and Hungarian-language teacher identities. Teacher value-added estimated from within-class score gains. Sample size ~ thousands of pupils + hundreds of teachers per district.
policy_relevance: Direct input for Hungarian education quality-equity policy (KIM, EMMI). The finding that intra-school class assignment subtly favours better-background classes is a tractable equity gap to close. Possible policy levers: school-level monitoring of teacher-class assignments by class background, with explicit equity-oriented review. Also useful for KH (Klebelsberg Központ) school-management practice and for principals' professional training.

title: Are separate classrooms inherently unequal? The effect of within-school sorting on the socioeconomic test score gap in Hungary
summary_en: Even within the same school, students from advantaged and disadvantaged families often end up in different classrooms. Does this within-school sorting matter? This paper uses universal test-score data for 6th and 8th graders in Hungary. Exploiting school fixed effects and quasi-random variation in sorting induced by enrollment and class-size rules, the authors show that sorting has a significant and economically meaningful effect on socioeconomic test-score gaps. Sorting harms low-status students but helps high-status students little or not at all. A clear empirical case against within-school class-composition segregation.
data_used: Universal-coverage administrative test-score data for Hungarian 6th and 8th graders. Exploits school fixed effects and quasi-exogenous variation from enrollment/class-size rules.
policy_relevance: Directly actionable for Hungarian education policy (Oktatási Hivatal, EMMI). The paper provides evidence for Ministry of Education rules against within-school socioeconomic sorting: regulations that prevent class-composition segregation improve outcomes for disadvantaged students without measurably harming advantaged ones. Particularly relevant to Hungary's Roma-education inclusion efforts. Caveat: the effect is identified at a specific grade; long-run impacts into high-school and labour-market outcomes are for future research.

title: Immigrant–native pay gap driven by lack of access to high-paying jobs
summary_en: Why do immigrants earn less than natives in rich countries? This paper uses linked employer-employee data from nine European and North American countries to separate two channels: (a) unequal pay for the same work at the same employer, and (b) immigrants being sorted into lower-paying jobs. The striking result: job sorting accounts for about three-quarters of the immigrant-native earnings gap. Within-job pay inequality exists and matters, but unequal access to higher-paying employers and positions is the dominant driver. Policy implications shift accordingly: addressing hiring and promotion barriers matters more than equal-pay enforcement.
data_used: Linked employer-employee administrative data from 9 countries (including Hungary, via boza-istvan). Covers 2 billion+ job-years nested within 50 million+ workplace-years. Enables decomposition of earnings gaps into within-job and between-job components.
policy_relevance: Highly relevant for Hungarian integration policy. The paper shows that closing immigrant-native pay gaps requires tackling job-access barriers — credential recognition, language programs, occupation licensing, network-based hiring — more than wage-discrimination enforcement. Relevant to ETDA, BM migration policy, and employer-level diversity efforts. Hungary-specific estimates (via Boza's KRTK work) are embedded in the sample. Caveat: sample is 9 countries; Hungarian context includes specific Roma-employment barriers that are a different case from typical immigrant-native dynamics.

title: Cycles and chaos in a socialist economy
summary_en: Can a planned economy generate endogenous business cycles — and even chaos — purely from its planning rules? Hommes, Nusse and Simonovits build a stylised dynamic model of a centrally-planned ('socialist') economy with adaptive output targets and show that the resulting investment cycle can exhibit endogenous oscillations and chaotic dynamics for plausible parameter ranges. The paper formalised long-running narrative claims (Kornai-style) about cyclical dysfunction under central planning into a rigorous nonlinear-dynamics framework.
data_used: Theoretical / numerical paper. Numerical illustrations use stylised Hungarian and Eastern-European socialist-era output series; formal results derive from the planning-rule dynamic system.
