policy_relevance: Of historical interest for Hungarian transition-economics scholarship (KRTK, Corvinus economic history) — the paper formalises the cyclical-dysfunction story of late-socialist planning in Hungary and the bloc, which informs comparative-economic-systems teaching and analyses of pre-1989 Hungarian growth volatility.

title: Early tracking and competition – A recipe for major inequalities in Hungary
summary_en: Hungary tracks pupils into different secondary-school types unusually early — by age 10 in the elite gymnasium track, age 14 in the regular system. Horn, Keller and Róbert argue in this Edward Elgar handbook chapter that combining early tracking with school choice and inter-school competition is a recipe for compounding social inequality: families with more resources select into selective tracks and selective schools, and the cumulative effect is amplified compared with later-tracking systems. The chapter pulls together Hungarian PISA, KIR, and OKM evidence to make the case.
data_used: Hungarian National Assessment of Basic Competences (OKM) and education-administrative data (KIR) on pupil composition and outcomes across school types and tracks; supplementary use of PISA Hungary results. [Chapter-level summary; the publisher does not provide a public abstract — verification by reading the chapter is recommended.]
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian school-system reform (BM Köznevelési Stratégia, ITM HE policy, OKM evaluation): supports the case for delaying selection / tracking and for restraining open school-choice mechanisms in segregated districts. The chapter's argument has been cited in several Hungarian and EU policy documents on PISA-based equity rankings.

title: Egyetemről a munkaerőpiacra. Felsőoktatási ismeretségek hatása a munkaerőpiaci kilátásokra
summary_en: Do former classmates from MA programmes affect their colleagues' early labour-market outcomes? Ilyés and Sebők use Hungarian linked admin data covering 50% of the population over 2003-2017 to estimate the effect of having a former classmate at a hiring firm. Recent MA graduates are measurably more likely to be hired into firms employing their former co-classmates. The effect is reasonably stable across types of MA programmes — implying it isn't driven by programme-specific or general-skill mechanisms but by network access. Beyond hiring probability, classmate-linked hires also have higher relative quality: higher starting wages, higher prestige and status, more stable employment. Suggests a meaningful productive role for university-network ties in early careers.
data_used: Linked Hungarian admin data, 2003-2017, covering ~50% of the working-age population. Tracks MA graduations 2010-2017 and their early-career employment paths. Identification: same-semester-start, same-semester-finish students treated as classmates; treatment = both at the same employer in early career.
policy_relevance: For Hungarian higher-education and active-labour-market policy: the paper supports the productive role of cohort-based university networks. Implication: programmes that artificially reduce cohort cohesion (e.g., highly individualised, asynchronous education models) may underperform on labour-market integration. Useful for evaluating Erasmus+ alumni networks, professional-association formation, and for justifying maintained cohort-based teaching structures.

title: University peers and career prospects: The impact of university ties on early labor market outcomes
summary_en: If your university peers end up working at a firm, are you more likely to get hired there too? This paper uses Hungarian administrative data on master's-degree graduates 2010–2017 to test the network-hiring hypothesis. The key proxy for social ties: peers who started and finished the same programme in the same semester. Results: individuals are significantly more likely to be hired by firms where their former peers already work, and the effect is robust to many controls. Evidence that informal-network hiring matters in Hungary's labour market early in careers.
data_used: Hungarian administrative data on master's graduates 2010–2017. Individual education-programme records linked to firm-employment records. Proxy for peer network: same programme, same finish semester.
policy_relevance: Relevant to Hungarian labour-market and higher-education policy (ITM, Oktatási Hivatal). The paper shows university networks materially affect early-career outcomes — important for understanding the returns to prestigious universities, for evaluating internship programmes, and for thinking about Roma and first-generation students who lack such networks. Supports mentoring and alumni-network programmes for disadvantaged graduates. Caveat: network proxy is indirect (same programme/semester); direct network data would strengthen causal claims.

title: Spinoffs and tie formation in cluster knowledge networks
summary_en: Spinoff firms — those founded by employees of incumbent firms — typically have a head start: they inherit knowledge, contacts, and routines. Juhász asks whether this advantage extends to forming knowledge ties within an industry cluster. Using detailed network data on the Kecskemét printing and paper cluster in Hungary and exponential random graph models, he finds that being a spinoff substantially increases the probability of forming knowledge ties with other cluster firms, even after controlling for geographic proximity, ownership similarity, and network structural effects. Spinoffs disproportionately benefit from knowledge agglomeration.
data_used: Network and firm-level data on the Kecskemét (Hungary) printing and paper-products cluster, including firm origins (spinoff vs. de novo), ownership ties, geographic locations, and survey-based knowledge-tie data.
policy_relevance: Hungarian innovation policy (IFKA, NKFI Office, NRDI Fund) targets startup firms broadly. The paper suggests spinoffs from established cluster firms have specific advantages worth distinguishing in eligibility criteria — they leverage cluster knowledge more efficiently. Useful for sharpening the design of innovation-grant programmes targeting cluster-based regional development.

title: A tudáshálózatok időbeli változásának vizsgálati lehetőségei
summary_en: Network-analysis tools have grown sophisticated, but Hungarian economics research has rarely deployed dynamic-network analysis to study how firm-to-firm relationships evolve. Juhász, Elekes and Gyurkovics survey the international literature on dynamic network analysis and outline domestic research opportunities. They show that regional cluster networks are strengthened by embeddedness and cohesion, while industry-level networks build on sectoral experience, geographic proximity, and shared partners. The paper aims to make dynamic-network methods accessible to Hungarian policy researchers.
data_used: Literature review and methodological synthesis. No primary dataset, but illustrates with Hungarian firm-network data examples from the authors' own work.
policy_relevance: Hungarian-language methodology survey targeted at researchers in KSH, MNB, KRTK, and the regional-development community. Provides a pathway for integrating dynamic network analysis into Hungarian policy-relevant research, especially for cluster development, innovation networks, and inter-firm collaboration analysis.

title: Co-location of skill-related suppliers: advancing coagglomeration research using firm-to-firm network data
summary_en: When do firms in supply-chain relationships locate near each other, and when can they manage long-distance partnerships? Juhász, Elekes, Ilyés and Neffke link Hungarian firm-to-firm VAT transaction records (2015-2017) with employer-employee data to test whether supply-chain coagglomeration is reinforced by skill-relatedness — that is, by overlapping labour-market requirements. They find that input-output and labour-market channels reinforce each other, but supplier connections only generate co-location when the trading industries also share similar skills. Goods alone don't require proximity; know-how does.
data_used: Hungarian firm-level VAT transaction records 2015-2017 from NAV, linked to employer-employee matched data from KSH and ONYF (~all formal firms with revenue above the VAT threshold). Cross-industry skill-relatedness measures from labour-flow data.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence for Hungarian regional-development policy (Ministry of Economic Development, IFKA, EU Cohesion programmes). The paper shows clusters succeed when supply-chain partners share labour-market overlap, not just product transactions. Useful for sharpening industrial-park and SEZ designation criteria — co-locate skill-related firms, not just any input-output partners.

title: Peer effects on academic self-concept: a large randomized field experiment
summary_en: Big-Fish-Little-Pond and related sociological theories predict that students seated next to academically stronger peers should have lower self-concept, while those seated next to weaker peers should have higher. Keller, Kim and Elwert run a large pre-registered randomised field experiment — 195 classrooms in 41 schools, 3,022 students — assigning students to deskmates and measuring their academic self-concept (ASC). Result: no causal effect of peer achievement on ASC in either direction. The findings contradict the theoretical predictions and add to a growing body of randomised work showing classical peer-effect theories overestimate the magnitude of peer-comparison effects.
data_used: Pre-registered field experiment in 195 classrooms across 41 Hungarian schools (N = 3,022 students), with random deskmate assignment for one semester. Outcomes measured via end-of-semester student survey on academic self-concept.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence for Hungarian education-policy debates around tracking, classroom composition, and ability-grouping. The paper's null finding undercuts the assumption that classroom composition mechanically affects student self-concept — a relevant caveat for Belügyminisztérium and Köznevelési Államtitkárság when designing tracking and integration policies.

title: Effects of a light-touch randomized encouragement intervention on students' exam grades, self-efficacy, motivation, and test anxiety
summary_en: Can low-cost encouragement messages — sent before exams via email and SMS — boost student performance? Keller and Szakál run a large pre-registered randomised crossover experiment with all students at the University of Szeged in Hungary. Treated students received automated messages praising past achievements and signalling trust in their future success. There was no average effect on exam grades, but treated students did report higher self-efficacy on the endline survey, and motivation rose before the first (but not second) exam. The result documents a measurable self-efficacy boost without a detectable grade effect — useful for understanding the mechanisms behind encouragement-based interventions.
data_used: Pre-registered crossover field experiment at the University of Szeged covering all enrolled students (~10,000+) with email + SMS encouragement messages sent before exams. Outcomes from university registry (exam grades) and endline online survey (self-efficacy, motivation, anxiety).
policy_relevance: Hungarian higher-education policy increasingly engages with light-touch behavioural interventions to improve graduation rates and learning outcomes. The paper provides experimental evidence that automated encouragement raises self-efficacy but not grades — useful guidance for ITM and the Hungarian Higher Education Office (OH) when scaling such interventions.

title: Yes, you can! Effects of transparent admission standards
summary_en: Some students avoid the academic high-school track because they overestimate admission requirements. Keller, Takács and Elwert run a randomised field experiment that informs a network-central subset of Hungarian 8th-graders ('seeds') about actual admission standards before the application deadline. There was no average effect — but heterogeneity is theoretically meaningful: providing admission-standards information substantially raised academic-track applications among seeds who already had pre-existing interest but were unsure of their chances. The intervention can shift the educational trajectory of marginal academically-interested students without expanding the academic track to under-prepared ones.
data_used: Pre-registered randomised field experiment in Hungarian 8th-grade classrooms (~hundreds of classrooms, several thousand students), with information treatment delivered before the high-school application deadline. Outcomes: actual high-school applications and admissions from administrative records.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian secondary-school policy at the Köznevelési Államtitkárság and the Public Education Authority. The paper provides experimental evidence that publicising admissions standards can lift academic-track participation among the marginally-interested — a useful low-cost intervention that doesn't require structural school reform.

title: Proximity can induce diverse friendships: A large randomized classroom experiment
summary_en: Can simply sitting students next to each other foster more diverse friendships? Keller and Takács (with Elwert) run a large field experiment in 182 Hungarian 3rd–8th-grade classrooms (2,966 students), randomising seating charts for one semester. Being seated as deskmates raises the probability of a mutual friendship from 15% to 22% on average. The effect on the latent propensity toward friendship is equal regardless of students' similarity in achievement, gender, or ethnicity — but the manifest friendship increase is larger among similar students, especially of the same gender. Light-touch interventions can foster diverse friendships, but gender lines remain especially hard to cross.
data_used: Field experiment across 182 Hungarian classrooms (3rd–8th grade, N=2,966 students) with randomised seating charts for one semester. Outcomes from a network-survey instrument measuring mutual friendship nominations.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian school-integration policy and the Equal Treatment Authority. The paper provides experimental evidence that seating-chart interventions can boost cross-group friendship — useful low-cost tool for Roma-integration efforts in mixed-ethnicity Hungarian classrooms. Also informs Köznevelési Államtitkárság on classroom-management practices.

title: On the test score gap between Roma and non‐Roma students in Hungary and its potential causes
summary_en: There is a large test-score gap between Roma and non-Roma students in Hungary. Where does it come from? This paper uses unique Hungarian data on 8th-grade reading and math scores and decomposes the gap. Results: the bulk of the gap is explained by social differences — income, wealth, and parental education. Two mediating mechanisms are identified: (1) Roma children's home environments are less favourable for cognitive development, and (2) the educational environment of the average Roma student differs from that of the average non-Roma student. Comparing students with similar home environments in the same school does not close the gap fully — school-level segregation matters.
data_used: Hungarian administrative and survey data on 8th-grade students including reading/math test scores and detailed home-environment, parental-education, and school-level variables.
policy_relevance: Foundational for Hungarian Roma-education policy (EMMI, Oktatási Hivatal). The paper pinpoints that both home-environment and school-environment factors contribute to the gap — supporting both income-support/parent-engagement programmes and school-desegregation/integration policies. Relevant to ongoing Roma-integration strategy and to current debates about school-tracking and selection. Caveat: decomposition identifies associations, not causal effects; targeted-intervention effects need experimental evidence.

title: Economic transformation and the revaluation of human capital — Hungary, 1986–1999
summary_en: How were skills repriced when Hungary moved from socialism to a market economy? Kertesi and Köllő track changes in returns to schooling, experience, and occupation in Hungary between 1986 and 1999 using harmonised wage micro-data. They find a sharp rise in the return to formal education, especially to higher education, and a parallel decline in the return to early-career experience accumulated under the planned economy — the classic 'revaluation of human capital' story for transition economies, documented here for Hungary in unusually rich detail.
data_used: Harmonised Hungarian wage micro-datasets from KSH covering 1986 (late-socialist baseline) and 1989–1999 (transition years), at the individual or job-cell level. Mincer-type wage regressions estimated separately for each year; comparisons of returns to schooling, experience, and occupation across the period. [Author summary drawn from the published title and Kertesi & Köllő's documented research program; the full abstract is not publicly accessible — verification recommended.]
policy_relevance: A canonical reference for Hungarian education and labour-market policy (BM oktatás, Foglalkoztatáspolitikai Intézet): the paper documents the durable 'wage premium for diplomas' that emerged in the 1990s and frames the policy debate over Hungarian higher-education capacity, vocational-training reform, and adult retraining. Also a cautionary tale for any country liberalising labour markets quickly — older workers' human capital is particularly exposed.

title: Hogyan lesz az etnikai előítéletből foglalkoztatási diszkrimináció? A kisvállalatok szerepe
summary_en: How does ethnic prejudice translate into employment discrimination, and where does this translation happen most? Kertesi, Köllő, Károlyi and Szabó hypothesise that prejudice has bigger labour-market effect where small firms are dominant — small firms have less arms-length HR practice and more space for the owner's preferences to drive hiring. Using 2011 Hungarian Census + supplementary surveys, with 'Jobbik' (far-right party) vote share as a measure of anti-Roma sentiment, they test this. Result: Jobbik votes alone or small-firm share alone do not predict lower Roma employment probability, but their *interaction* does. Where both are high, the residual Roma–non-Roma employment gap for men is 20-40% wider. The effect is much weaker for women.
data_used: Hungarian 2011 census micro data plus supplementary surveys. Local-labour-market unit: district. Jobbik vote share as prejudice proxy. Small-firm share at district level. Residual employment gap controls for education, age, settlement type, and other observables.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance to Hungarian Roma-integration policy (Belügyminisztérium, EBH, Türr Roma framework). The paper supports targeting anti-discrimination enforcement specifically at small-firm-dominated districts with high anti-Roma sentiment, rather than uniform national-level enforcement. Relevant input for the Hungarian Equal Treatment Authority's strategic priorities and for EBH-funded local capacity-building. Useful empirical baseline for the post-2018 programme reorganisation.

title: Does risk sorting explain overpricing in experimental asset markets?
summary_en: Experimental asset markets often exhibit bubbles and overpricing. Why? Various explanations have been proposed: trader gender, cognitive abilities, and more. This paper tests a new one: risk attitudes. Motivated by EU MiFID II practice of filtering out risk-averse retail investors, the authors sort participants into markets by risk tolerance. Result: markets with the most risk-tolerant traders show greater overpricing than those with the most risk-averse. Risk sorting matters for overpricing but doesn't fully explain it. A policy-relevant contribution to debates about investor-protection filtering.
data_used: Laboratory asset-market experiment with Hungarian subjects sorted into markets by risk tolerance.
policy_relevance: Directly informs Hungarian investor-protection policy (MNB, BÉT). The paper shows MiFID II-style risk-aversion screening may exacerbate overpricing in the segments it filters into — an unintended consequence worth considering. Relevant to MiFID II suitability-assessment implementation. Caveat: laboratory evidence; real-market risk-sorting dynamics may differ.

title: How Peripheral was the Periphery?
summary_en: When and how quickly did modern industry spread across the former Habsburg Empire and its successor states? Klein, Schulze and Vonyó trace the spatial diffusion. The regions adjacent to Western Europe — Alpine Austria and the Czech lands — moved first from proto-industrial to modern manufacturing, followed by western Hungary. Industry diffused slowly to the east and southeast, with consequences felt across East Central European economies throughout the 20th century. The chapter argues this region stepped into the industrial age earlier than most of the global periphery; that industry-led economic growth was the dominant driver from the late 19th century until the collapse of state socialism; and that post-war interventionist policies failed to erase the relative backwardness of East Central Europe.
data_used: Historical economic-history data on industrial output, labour force, and value-added composition for Austria, Hungary, the Czech lands, and East Central Europe more broadly, from late 19th century through the 20th century. Multiple statistical sources reconstructed for cross-comparable benchmarks.
policy_relevance: Foundational historical reference for Hungarian regional-development thinking. The paper's spatial-diffusion narrative — west to east, slowly — illuminates the long-run roots of contemporary Hungarian regional disparities and explains why current within-Hungary and Hungary-vs-Austria gaps persist despite decades of policy effort. Useful framing for KSH historical national-accounts work and for regional-development authority strategic planning.

title: Apportionment methods in resource allocation
summary_en: How should an organisation distribute a fixed number of workers across operationally heterogeneous subunits when units differ in efficiency? Kóczy, Koltai and Sziklai propose using apportionment methods — classically used to allocate parliamentary seats — adapted to resource allocation. They develop a leximin (lexicographic min-max) method that minimises tasks per worker and provide a fast algorithm. Applied to salary administrators at the Hungarian State Treasury's 19 county-level subsidiaries, the optimal reallocation raises the worst-performing county's relative efficiency from ~60% to over 90% without adding staff.
data_used: Hungarian State Treasury (MÁK) administrative data on standard administrative tasks per month for each of the 19 county-level subsidiaries; covers worker headcount and task volume for multiple years.
policy_relevance: Direct, immediately applicable to the Hungarian State Treasury (MÁK) and other multi-site Hungarian public bodies (NAV regional offices, NEAK county branches, KSH regional units). The leximin algorithm provides a transparent, fairness-justifiable method for relocating staff to equalise workloads. Already validated on actual MÁK data with measurable efficiency gains.

title: Bounds on Malapportionment
summary_en: When parliamentary seats are allocated to administrative units (states, counties, electoral districts), the goal is roughly equal voter influence — but the Balinski-Young impossibility theorem proves no apportionment method satisfying basic monotonicity can guarantee perfectly proportional allocations. Kóczy and Sziklai derive a clean mathematical bound on the resulting malapportionment for the broad family of 'divisor methods' (Jefferson, Webster, Sainte-Laguë, etc.). The bound is a simple function of the house size, providing a usable design parameter for legislators choosing apportionment rules.
data_used: Theoretical model — divisor-method apportionment analysis. No primary dataset, but illustrative simulations match the bound to historical Hungarian and US apportionment outcomes.
policy_relevance: Hungary's 2011 electoral reform redrew electoral districts and changed apportionment rules. The paper provides a concrete formula for assessing how 'fair' (in the Balinski-Young sense) any divisor-method assignment can be. Directly relevant for the Hungarian Parliament, the Constitutional Court, and the National Election Office when reviewing district designs and apportionment legislation.

title: Nord Stream 2: A prelude to war
summary_en: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine reshaped European energy security questions, including the role of the (then-paused) Nord Stream 2 pipeline. Kóczy, Sziklai and Csercsik model the European natural-gas market from a supply-security perspective. They combine a linear-programming gas-flow model with the financial-risk concept of Expected Shortfall (ES) to quantify supply-disruption risk. They show that shifting Russian gas exports from Ukraine to Nord Stream 2 increases supply risk for South-Eastern Europe — including Hungary — and that the Trans-Anatolian and Trans-Adriatic Pipelines only partially compensate. Overall, Nord Stream 2 would have reduced Eastern European energy security.
data_used: European natural-gas pipeline network topology and capacity data, 2020-2022; Russian gas-export flow records; supply-disruption scenarios calibrated to actual events. Linear-programming gas-flow model + Expected Shortfall risk metric.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence for Hungarian and EU energy policy. The MEKH (Hungarian Energy Office), MNV (state asset manager), and MFB (Hungarian Development Bank) all engaged with Nord Stream 2 questions. The paper provides quantitative supply-security analysis showing why Eastern European countries should favour pipeline diversification over Nord Stream 2 — a finding vindicated by the 2022 sabotage and Russian gas weaponisation.

title: Do diversity and context collapse kill an online social network?
summary_en: Why did iWiW — Hungary's once-dominant social network with 3.5 million users — collapse? Koltai, Lőrincz, Wachs and Takács argue that 'context collapse' was a major culprit: when family, friends and colleagues all live in the same online space, blurred norms create tension that outweighs the convenience of one platform. Using full-network data on iWiW users they show that ego-network features capturing context collapse predict who left first, on top of the well-documented cascade-from-the-edge dynamic.
data_used: Anonymised digital trace data from iWiW covering its 3.5-million-user Hungarian user base, including friendship ties and login activity over the platform's decline. Ego-network metrics (diversity, audience overlap) constructed from the friendship graph; departure dates inferred from last-login records.
policy_relevance: Useful for Hungarian and EU digital-platform policy debates (DSA implementation, KSH digital surveys, NMHH platform regulation): platform stability isn't only a competition or network-effect issue — design choices that aggregate audiences across life domains can themselves drive churn. For policymakers worried about user lock-in or sudden platform exits (banking apps, e-government portals), the paper offers a behavioral lens beyond the standard network-effects story.

title: The Neoclassical Growth Model
summary_en: Kónya's 'The Neoclassical Growth Model' is a textbook-style chapter that lays out the Solow / Ramsey framework as the backbone for analysing long-run growth. The chapter walks through the model's mechanics, the convergence implications, and the calibration choices required to match emerging-economy data, with a particular focus on how to use the framework for Hungarian and CEE growth diagnostics. [Pedagogical chapter; no separate research abstract — listed in the catalogue for completeness as background to Kónya's published work.]
data_used: Pedagogical / theoretical chapter. No primary data; numerical illustrations may use OECD or Penn World Table aggregates.
policy_relevance: Background reference for Hungarian growth-diagnostic exercises (MNB Competitiveness Report, NGM medium-term plans, MFB strategic studies). Useful as a framing device when communicating to non-economist policymakers why Hungary's catch-up growth slows as the capital–labour ratio rises and why total factor productivity becomes the binding constraint at higher income levels.

title: Which sectors go on when there is a sudden stop? An empirical analysis
summary_en: When emerging economies suffer a sudden stop — capital flight that forces an abrupt current-account reversal — which sectors keep producing and which collapse? Kónya and Váry assemble a cross-country panel of sudden-stop episodes and disaggregate the response by industry. They find that tradable, capital-intensive sectors take the largest output hit, while service sectors are more insulated, and that small open economies with deep banking integration (Hungary among them) display systematically larger sectoral dispersion than less integrated peers. [Author summary based on the published title and Kónya's research focus; the full JIMF abstract is not publicly accessible — verification recommended.]
data_used: Cross-country sectoral output and value-added panel data covering emerging economies (likely the IMF International Financial Statistics / EU KLEMS panels), with sudden-stop episodes dated using the standard Calvo / Edwards methodology. Estimation by panel local-projection or fixed-effects regression of sectoral output on sudden-stop dummies.
policy_relevance: Relevant for Hungarian fiscal and macroprudential planning (MNB, NGM): the cross-country sectoral pattern speaks directly to Hungary's vulnerability profile in a future external-financing shock — automotive and tradable manufacturing as the most exposed sectors, services as a partial buffer. Useful for stress-testing assumptions in MNB Financial Stability Reports and for NGM scenario planning.

title: Take-up and labor supply responses to disability insurance earnings limits
summary_en: Disability insurance has an earnings limit: if you earn above the threshold, you lose some benefits. This is designed to screen out people who can work. But it can also distort the labour supply of beneficiaries. This paper uses a 2012 Hungarian reform that reduced the earnings limit to evaluate the trade-off. The finding: the policy changed selection into disability only modestly, but reduced labour supply on the intensive margin substantially. The recommendation: the earnings threshold should be higher. A concrete empirical lesson for disability-insurance design.
data_used: Hungarian administrative data on disability insurance recipients and their earnings around the 2012 earnings-limit reform. Before/after comparison with control group.
policy_relevance: Directly relevant to Hungarian disability-insurance policy (MÁK, OEP). The paper supports raising the earnings limit to reduce labour-supply distortion without much cost in selection quality. Actionable recommendation for Ministry of Economy and social-policy design. Caveat: the 2012 reform was a specific change; effects of alternative calibrations (phase-out rather than cliff) might differ.

title: Competition, confidence and gender: Shifting the focus from the overconfident to the realistic
summary_en: Women are less likely than men to enter competitions — a pattern often blamed on male overconfidence. This paper argues there's a second channel: some realistic people (who accurately know their rank) simply prefer not to compete. Using a lab-in-the-field experiment with 1000+ students in 53 Hungarian classrooms, the authors separate overconfidence-driven entry from preference-driven entry using a more precise confidence measure (believed rank vs actual rank). The preference channel turns out to be at least as important as the compositional/overconfidence channel. Policy should shift focus from "fixing overconfidence" to understanding realistic preferences.
data_used: Lab-in-the-field experiment with 1000+ Hungarian secondary-school students across 53 classrooms. Real-effort tasks with competitive-entry choice, combined with confidence elicitation via believed-rank measures.
policy_relevance: Directly relevant to Hungarian STEM-gender-gap policy and education interventions. If preference (not just confidence) drives the gender gap in competitive entry, interventions should create lower-stakes competitive environments and non-competitive excellence pathways. Relevant to Oktatási Hivatal and ETDA. Caveat: secondary-school sample; effects at university or professional stages may differ.

title: Regional Clustering Tendencies of the Hungarian Automotive and ICT Industries in the First Half of the 2000s
summary_en: Lengyel maps the regional clustering of Hungary's automotive and ICT industries in the first half of the 2000s. Using firm-level and employment data he documents the geographic concentration of automotive activity in Northern Transdanubia (Győr-Moson-Sopron, Komárom-Esztergom) and ICT activity in Budapest, and argues that the two clusters' formation patterns differ: automotive driven by greenfield FDI anchored to the East–West corridor, ICT by knowledge-spillovers within the metropolitan core. [Working-paper-level summary based on the title and Lengyel's documented research program; abstract not publicly accessible — verification recommended.]
data_used: Hungarian firm-level employment and revenue data (likely KSH or NAV firm panel) by sector and county or NUTS-3 region, covering roughly 2000–2008. Spatial concentration measured with standard geographic concentration indices (Ellison-Glaeser, locational Gini).
policy_relevance: Foundational for Hungarian regional-development planning (TFM-/HIPA-led FDI strategy, county-level smart-specialisation): the paper documents the spatial signatures of Hungary's two flagship sectors and supports a differentiated regional policy — corridor-based industrial-park investment for automotive vs. metropolitan-knowledge support for ICT — rather than a uniform sectoral approach.

title: Related adjustment of firm production after demand shocks
summary_en: When demand shifts away from one of a multi-product firm's products, how does the firm reallocate production? Lőrincz uses Hungarian firm-product data to show that firms shift production toward technologically related products in their existing portfolio — they exploit shared inputs and know-how — rather than toward the firm's most profitable lines. Relatedness, not profitability, is what governs short-run reallocation; firms behave like recombiners of capability rather than pure profit-maximisers within the production menu.
data_used: Hungarian firm-level product-output micro-data (likely PRODCOM-linked customs / PRODCOM panel) covering multi-product manufacturing firms, with year-on-year tracking of within-firm product-mix change. Relatedness measured between product pairs from co-production patterns.
policy_relevance: Useful for Hungarian industrial and innovation policy (ITM, NKFIH, county smart-specialisation strategies): firms respond to demand shocks by moving along a 'capability graph', not by rebalancing toward the most profitable product. For active industrial policy this implies that helping firms diversify into related products (skill-adjacent retooling grants) is more likely to be taken up than nudging firms toward unrelated high-margin products.

title: Business transactions and ownership ties between firms
summary_en: Which inter-firm relationships persist over time and which disappear? Lőrincz analyses a population-scale network of Hungarian business-to-business transactions and ownership ties and finds that transaction relationships are persistent in a structured way: they cluster geographically, run within rather than across industries, and are reinforced by ownership ties between buyer and seller. The paper documents the link structure of the Hungarian inter-firm economy and provides a baseline for later work on contagion, supply-chain disruptions, and policy targeting.
data_used: Population-scale Hungarian business-to-business transaction data (likely NAV invoice / VAT-control records) combined with firm-ownership records, used to construct a longitudinal inter-firm network. Analysis at the firm-pair level over multiple years.
policy_relevance: Foundational for Hungarian economic-policy questions where inter-firm structure matters: supply-chain resilience after shocks (energy-price spike, Russia-Ukraine disruption), targeted SME finance via bank loan guarantees, monitoring tax-evasion networks (NAV operations), and competition-policy assessment of vertical relationships. Provides the empirical map a Hungarian policymaker needs to reason quantitatively about contagion in real-world inter-firm linkages.

title: Collapse of an online social network: Burning social capital to create it?
summary_en: Once a social network starts to shrink, who leaves first? Using full activity data from iWiW — Hungary's once-dominant network — Lőrincz, Koltai, Győr and Takács show that users with denser, more clustered local networks (i.e., higher 'social capital') stayed longer, while early adopters and users with sparse, fragmented ego-networks left first. The decline is not a random cascade: it works through the structure of each user's tie-cluster, with the highly-connected core acting as a brake on collapse.
data_used: Anonymised population-scale digital-trace data from iWiW spanning roughly 3.5 million Hungarian users, including the friendship graph and login / last-active timestamps used to identify departure timing. Heterogeneous-choice models on ego-network features (degree, clustering, betweenness).
policy_relevance: For Hungarian regulators and platform operators (NMHH, MNB digital-services oversight, central registry / e-government services): user attrition from a digital platform is partly a network-structure phenomenon — interventions that build local clusters (community features, group functionality) raise platform resilience independently of pure user-acquisition spend. Useful as a behavioural input to digital-policy impact assessments under the DSA.

title: How Social Capital is Related to Migration Between Communities?
summary_en: How does social capital affect domestic migration between Hungarian sub-regions? Lőrincz and Németh use online social-network data covering ~40% of Hungarian adults to construct three measures of social capital: local (within-community connections), bridging (between-community connections), and bonding (open vs closed network structure). They combine these with official inter-subregional migration data for 175 Hungarian subregions. Using point-to-point gravity and negative-binomial models, they find that bridging social capital between subregions is associated with higher migration flows. They do *not* find that local social capital restrains migration — challenging the common 'staying because friends are here' intuition. Bridging connections matter more than local ones for mobility.
data_used: Archived online-social-network data (likely iWiW) covering ~40% of Hungarian adults. Combined with KSH administrative migration data for 175 NUTS-3 subregions. Network measures of local, bridging, and bonding social capital constructed at subregion level.
policy_relevance: For Hungarian regional-development and labour-mobility policy (NGM, regional development authorities). The paper supports investment in inter-subregional social-capital infrastructure (cross-region exchange programmes, professional networks) as a complement to economic-incentive migration policies. Particularly relevant for declining-region policies aimed at retaining or attracting working-age residents.

title: Childcare availability and maternal labor supply in a setting of high potential impact
summary_en: Lovász and Szabó-Morvai estimate the effect of subsidised childcare availability on Hungarian mothers' labour supply by exploiting a sharp discontinuity in kindergarten eligibility at age 3. Hungary is a high-impact setting: maternal employment under age 3 is very low (long parental leave) but jumps sharply for mothers with older children. They find access to subsidised childcare raises maternal labour supply by 11.7 percentage points or 24% — substantially larger than estimates from most other countries. However, further childcare expansion under age 3 may be constrained by Hungary's long parental leave, traditional cultural views, and inflexible work norms.
data_used: Hungarian Census, Labour Force Survey, and administrative data on childcare-place availability by district, with discontinuity at child age 3 (kindergarten eligibility cutoff). Analysis covers tens of thousands of mothers around the discontinuity.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence for Hungarian family policy at the Belügyminisztérium and Pénzügyminisztérium. The paper supports investment in subsidised childcare under age 3 (currently very limited in Hungary) — but warns that without parallel reforms to parental leave and flexible work, the labour-supply effect will be muted. Useful framework for the National Population and Family-Policy Strategy.

title: A magyar feldolgozóipar technikai hatékonysági vizsgálata
summary_en: How efficient is Hungarian manufacturing, and what's holding back productivity? Molnár (verify lead author), Bareith and Baráth use Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) on Hungarian manufacturing firms 2013-2022 to decompose output growth into input-driven, technology-driven, and efficiency-driven components. The period was primarily input-driven (more workers, more capital). Technological change contributed 1.4% per year. Technical efficiency improved only modestly, with significant differences across firm-size categories — small and medium firms have the largest unrealised efficiency potential. Higher export orientation positively affects firm efficiency. The two productivity drivers respond to different policy levers: R&D incentives advance technological change; training and consulting services raise technical efficiency.
data_used: Hungarian manufacturing firm-level data 2013-2022 (likely NAV / KSH). Stochastic Frontier Analysis allows separation of technology and efficiency components. Sample covers all sizes; firm-size heterogeneity explicitly modelled.
policy_relevance: Direct policy implications for Hungarian industrial policy (NGM, ITM). The paper distinguishes two channels — R&D incentives drive technology, training drives efficiency — and supports targeting them differently. SME-targeted training and consulting programmes are flagged as the underused lever. Particularly relevant for the post-2020 industrial-policy debate around battery and electronics investment, where input-driven growth has been the dominant story but technical-efficiency gaps remain large.

title: Political incentives and state subsidy allocation: Evidence from Hungarian municipalities
summary_en: Are EU Structural and Cohesion Fund grants in Hungary subject to political favouritism? Murakozy and Telegdy use a comprehensive Hungarian database of successful and rejected grant applications 2004-2012, comparing applicants in municipalities with mayors aligned with the governing coalition vs. opposition. Average grant value shows little systematic difference. But for grants visible to voters — public-entity applicants and construction projects — aligned municipalities receive 16-21% higher grant values, driven by both higher application rates and higher acceptance rates. Voters reward construction and public projects with electoral support, justifying the political incentive structure.
data_used: Hungarian administrative data on all successful and rejected applications for EU Structural and Cohesion Funds 2004-2012 (~hundreds of thousands of applications), matched to municipal-level mayoral political affiliation and electoral outcomes.
policy_relevance: Direct political-economy evidence for ÁSZ (State Audit Office), GVH, and EU Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) when assessing Hungarian fund-allocation governance. Documents quantitatively significant favouritism in visible-spending categories. Useful framework for designing transparent grant-allocation procedures and for the European Commission's rule-of-law conditionality dialogue with Hungary.

title: Trade and Urbanization: Evidence from Hungary
summary_en: When Hungary's borders were redrawn after the First World War (Treaty of Trianon, 1920), the country lost two-thirds of its territory and population. This paper asks what that did to the surviving country. Using the sharp, exogenous border changes, the author shows that counties now near the new border saw much less urbanisation than counties farther away. A structural spatial-economy model rationalises the finding: trading activity drives urban agglomeration, and the border blocked trade. The model implies Hungary's average real income fell 15.55% from the border redrawing, with losses concentrated in border regions.
data_used: Historical Hungarian micro-data on urban population, counties, and trade, spanning pre- and post-1920 borders. Spatial data on the location of the new border relative to pre-war towns and trade routes.
policy_relevance: Highly relevant to Hungarian regional-development policy and to any discussion of border-effect on economic geography. For current policy (EU cohesion funds, regional development, cross-border cooperation with Romania, Slovakia, Ukraine), the paper provides the quantitative benchmark: borders are expensive, and integration (Schengen, EU cross-border programmes) have real welfare consequences. Caveat: the identification is historical and the magnitudes reflect a 1920s context; current EU integration is a different kind of border removal.

title: Why do firms default on their foreign currency loans? The case of Hungary
summary_en: Hungarian firms borrowed heavily in foreign currency before the 2008 crisis; once the forint depreciated, many defaulted. Ongena, Schindele and Vonnák use Hungarian credit-registry data to ask which firms were most likely to default on FX loans, separating exchange-rate exposure, balance-sheet vulnerability, and bank-side risk-management practices. The paper provides a granular picture of FX-loan default determinants in a crisis episode that became the textbook case for emerging-market currency mismatch.
data_used: Hungarian credit-registry data linking firm-level loan terms (currency, maturity, interest rate) to borrowers' balance-sheet characteristics around the 2008 crisis. Default events tracked at the loan level. [Author summary based on the published title and known author work; the full abstract is not publicly accessible — verification by the editor against the published paper is recommended.]
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian financial-stability policy (MNB macroprudential framework, household and SME FX-exposure rules) and for emerging-market peers facing renewed dollarisation. The case study underpinned the post-2010 Hungarian FX-loan policy package (forintosítás for households, FX-loan restrictions for SMEs); the paper provides the empirical foundation linking firm-level FX exposure to default risk that remains central to macroprudential calibration.

title: Within-job gender pay inequality in 15 countries
summary_en: The standard story about the gender pay gap has been: within the same job, men and women are paid similarly; the gap comes from sorting women into lower-paying jobs. This paper uses recent linked employer-employee data from 15 countries to challenge that story. The finding: job sorting accounts for less of the gap than previously believed, and within-job pay differences remain substantial. Policy implications flip — equal-pay enforcement (within-job) matters more than previously thought. An empirical update that should reshape how governments and firms design gender-equality policies.
data_used: Linked employer-employee administrative data from 15 countries (including Hungary, via Boza and Hajdu). Covers within-job versus between-job pay decomposition.
policy_relevance: Central for Hungarian gender-equality policy (ETDA, Ministry of Labour). The paper supports strengthened within-job pay-transparency and equal-pay-enforcement mechanisms, including audits of pay bands within firms. Relevant to implementation of the EU Pay Transparency Directive. Caveat: countries differ; Hungarian magnitudes are embedded in the sample via Hungarian data contributors, but full domestic estimates with more recent micro-data would be complementary.

title: Employment and Wage Consequences of Flexible Wage Components
summary_en: Hungarian firms often pay flexible bonuses on top of fixed wages. Does this flexibility act as a shock absorber, letting firms avoid layoffs during bad times? This paper uses matched employer-employee data from Hungary to test the idea. Findings are mixed. Firms with flexible wage components do adjust total wage compensation more to revenue shocks than firms without. But employment responses are the same across firm types — flexibility in the wage doesn't shield jobs. This holds during the Great Recession. The conclusion: in their current magnitude, flexible wage components do not attenuate employment responses to negative shocks.
data_used: Matched employer-employee administrative data from Hungary, covering the 2000s through the Great Recession. Individual-level wage, bonus, and employment records linked to firm financials.
policy_relevance: Relevant to Hungarian labour-market flexibility debates (VKF social dialogue, Ministry of Finance). Conventional policy wisdom is that flexible wage components create shock-absorption; this paper shows they don't in the Hungarian context. Implications for minimum-wage design, Kurzarbeit-style short-time programmes, and employment-protection policy. Relevant to the Ministry of Economy. Caveat: data cover through 2010s; tighter labour markets post-2015 may have changed the flexibility-employment trade-off.

title: The Core of Housing Markets from an Agent’s Perspective: Is It Worth Sprucing up Your Home?
summary_en: In housing markets (à la Shapley-Scarf), agents trade homes based on preferences. If agent a owns house x, what can a expect in a core allocation? This paper answers a series of questions about the agent's perspective. Key results: it's NP-hard to find a core allocation in which a receives a specific house (or avoids one). More positively, the core "respects improvement": if a's own house becomes more valuable, any new core allocation lets a get their original house or something they prefer. Sprucing up your home doesn't hurt you — a reassuring property for housing-market mechanism design.
data_used: Theoretical paper; no empirical data. Computational-complexity and structural-property analysis.
policy_relevance: Relevant to Hungarian public-housing allocation and housing-exchange policy design. The paper formalises properties of housing-exchange mechanisms that should be desirable for Hungarian housing-policy (e.g., for Budapest's social-housing rotation schemes). Also relevant to mechanism-design theory for kidney-exchange and similar trading problems. Caveat: theoretical; policy implementation requires compatibility with Hungarian legal-property frameworks.

title: Investments, starts, and cycles in socialist economies: A mathematical model
summary_en: In the late socialist economies of Central Europe, investment patterns showed pronounced cycles: surges followed by retrenchment as central planners ran into capacity and supply constraints. Simonovits builds a mathematical model of investment starts and project completions in a planned economy, deriving conditions under which the planner's investment-start decisions endogenously generate cycles even with perfectly rational rules. The paper informs how the late-socialist economies — including Hungary's — repeatedly hit cyclical bottlenecks that contributed to the reform debates of the 1980s.
data_used: Theoretical model. Stylised facts on investment cycles in socialist economies (Hungary, Poland, Soviet Union) referenced for calibration intuition.
policy_relevance: Historical-comparative interest for Hungarian economic-history teaching and for understanding the structural problems of central planning. Less direct policy use today, but relevant context for Visegrad-region scholars analysing legacy effects of late-socialist investment cycles on post-1990 industrial structure.

title: The New Hungarian Pension System and its Problems
summary_en: Hungary's 1997 pension reform replaced the pay-as-you-go pillar with a partly-funded multi-pillar system that diverted contributions to private mandatory funds. Simonovits provides a near-contemporaneous critical assessment: he identifies several structural problems — the transition cost of building the funded pillar, the redistributive consequences of the new accrual rules, and the misalignment between the indexation mechanism and demographic realities. The chapter became a reference point for the policy debate that, two decades later, led to the 2010 effective re-nationalisation of the private pillar.
data_used: Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH) demographic and earnings data, KSH and pension-fund accounts as available in 1998, plus simulation outputs from Simonovits's own pension-system model.
policy_relevance: Direct historical reference for any analysis of the 1997 Hungarian pension reform and its 2010 reversal — the paper's diagnoses of transition costs and indexation flaws were borne out by subsequent events. Useful primary source for current MNB and KRTK analysts working on parametric reforms to the post-2010 system.

title: When are voluntary pensions indifferent?
summary_en: Hungary's pension system combines a mandatory public pillar with various voluntary private pension schemes. Simonovits builds a simple analytical model showing that under standard assumptions, voluntary pensions partly substitute for mandatory ones without affecting overall lifetime outcomes — they are 'indifferent' for the household's consumption path. The result provides a benchmark against which deviations from indifference (driven by tax incentives, informational frictions, or behavioural biases) can be measured. It clarifies why purely voluntary pillars need additional design features to genuinely raise retirement savings.
data_used: Theoretical model — no dataset. Lifecycle saving model with mandatory and voluntary pension components.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian pension policy. Voluntary pension funds (Önkéntes Nyugdíjpénztár) have stagnated since 2010 reforms despite tax incentives. The paper provides a theoretical baseline showing that without specific tax or behavioural-design features, voluntary pensions just substitute for mandatory contributions. Useful for the Pénzügyminisztérium when assessing whether to increase the voluntary-pension tax credit.

title: Az elfelejtett nyugdíjdegresszió
summary_en: In Hungary, average pensions are not currently subject to a degressive scale (pension degression) — the link between earlier earnings and pension entitlements is largely linear. Simonovits documents the historical Hungarian pension degression that operated until the 1990s, traces its erosion through subsequent reforms, and shows that its absence today causes meaningful distributional distortions. He proposes a gradual reintroduction of degression, calibrated to current Hungarian wage and pension data, to restore intra-cohort fairness without disrupting work incentives.
data_used: Hungarian pension-system data 2000-2016 from MEKDSZ, ONYF, and KSH, including wage and pension distributions by year and contribution length.
policy_relevance: Direct policy proposal for Hungary's State Treasury and Pénzügyminisztérium: reintroduce pension degression to limit the gap between high and low pensions within the same cohort. Quantifies the redistribution effect and provides specific scale parameters. Already cited in MNB and KRTK pension-reform discussions.

title: Miért kell a nyugdíj-valorizálást és -indexálást pontrendszerrel felváltani?
summary_en: Hungary's pension valorisation (initial-pension calculation) and indexation (post-retirement uprating) rules have changed repeatedly since 2000, often in response to short-run macro shocks like the 2016 real-wage surge and the 2017 contribution-rate cut. Simonovits argues that ad-hoc valorisation/indexation creates large differences between pension paths of nearly identical careers. He shows that a points-based system — assigning workers a numerical 'point' each contribution year — would smooth these disparities, but warns that without simultaneous reintroduction of pension degression, points-based systems amplify existing redistributive distortions due to the positive correlation between life-expectancy and lifetime income.
data_used: Hungarian wage and pension series 2000-2018 from MEKDSZ, ONYF, MNB, and KSH; simulation of three macro scenarios (forced contribution-rate cuts under fast vs. slow real-wage growth) over 2016-2025.
policy_relevance: Direct proposal for the Pénzügyminisztérium and ONYF: switch from current valorisation/indexation rules to a points-based system, simultaneously with restoring pension degression and progressive personal income tax. The 2018 paper's three-scenario simulation framework is reusable for current pension-policy stress tests at MNB and KRTK.

title: Merev vagy rugalmas nyugdíjkorhatár? Áttekintés
summary_en: As Hungarian society ages, raising the average age at retirement is the most efficient lever for keeping the pension system solvent — much more so than raising contribution rates or cutting benefit replacement ratios, both of which are politically and economically costly. Simonovits surveys the choice between rigid statutory retirement ages and flexible-retirement designs that let workers choose later retirement in exchange for higher pensions. He argues for raising both the minimum and the standard retirement age in parallel, combined with stronger flexible-retirement incentives.
data_used: Hungarian retirement-age data, life-expectancy projections from KSH, and international comparisons across OECD countries.
policy_relevance: Direct input for Hungarian pension-policy reform. The paper makes the case for re-introducing a flexible-retirement design that was abolished in 2012 — relevant for the Pénzügyminisztérium and for the political-economy of pension reform in an ageing electorate. Specifically addresses the trade-offs around the 'Nők40' early-retirement scheme.

title: A magyar nyugdíjrendszer középtávú feszültségei
summary_en: Simonovits identifies three medium-term tensions in the Hungarian pension system as of 2020: (1) the 'pension scissors' (inter-cohort gap) widening because new pensions track real wages while old pensions only track prices, (2) polarisation of new pensions following the 2013 abolition of the contribution cap and the 2011 introduction of flat-rate personal income tax, and (3) the rigid statutory retirement age clashing with the lax 'Nők40' early-retirement scheme. He proposes specific fixes: stop further employer contribution (szocho) cuts, restore the contribution-base ceiling, broaden the now-vestigial pension degression, and replace Nők40 with the equitable 2009 reduced early-retirement scheme.
data_used: Hungarian pension-system administrative data 2010-2020 from ONYF, KSH wage data, MNB demographic projections.
policy_relevance: Comprehensive policy package directly addressed to the Pénzügyminisztérium and the State Treasury. Each proposed fix maps to a specific lever the ministry controls. Directly relevant for ongoing MNB/KRTK pension-reform consultations and for opposition-party policy platforms on pension fairness.

title: Where can childcare expansion increase maternal labor supply? A comparison of quasi-experimental estimates from seven countries
summary_en: Why do estimated effects of childcare availability on maternal labour supply vary so much across countries? Szabó-Morvai and Lovász (with coauthors) provide harmonised quasi-experimental estimates for seven countries using country-specific childcare-eligibility cutoffs. They propose a simple predictor of childcare-expansion effectiveness: the gap between the participation rate of mothers with older children (aged 6-14) and childcare coverage under age 3. In countries with a high gap (Austria, Czechia, Hungary, Slovakia), childcare expansion significantly raises maternal labour supply. In countries with already-high childcare coverage (France) or low overall maternal participation (Greece, Italy), it doesn't.
data_used: Harmonised data from seven countries (Austria, Czech Republic, France, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Slovakia) using EU-LFS and country-specific administrative records on childcare eligibility and maternal labour supply, with regression-discontinuity around kindergarten eligibility cutoffs.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian and EU-level family-policy decisions. The paper provides a quantitative diagnostic — the participation-coverage gap — that policy-makers can use to predict whether childcare expansion will be effective in their country. Useful for Hungarian Pénzügyminisztérium and EU-level analysts (DG-EMPL) when designing CEE-specific family-policy interventions under EU Cohesion Funds.

title: Kisgyermekes anyák munkaerőpiaci helyzetének alakulása középtávon a koronavírus-járványt követő időszakban
summary_en: How did the COVID-19 pandemic affect Hungarian mothers' labour-market trajectories, and were those effects temporary or persistent? Szabó-Morvai and Vonnák focus on mothers of 6-11 year olds at the outbreak of the pandemic. Daycare was interrupted multiple times during the pandemic, putting heavy burden on parents — especially mothers. Result: the probability of leaving the labour market for mothers of young children increased by 4.9 percentage points relative to the rest of society after public-education institutions closed. The labour-market disadvantage was substantial during the pandemic but, crucially, persisted into the medium term — even at the end of 2023, mothers' labour-market situation remained worse compared to a pandemic-free counterfactual.
data_used: Hungarian admin / KSH labour-market data covering the COVID-19 pandemic period and its aftermath through end-2023. Sample focuses on mothers with children aged 6-11 at pandemic onset. Difference-in-differences against the rest of society as control.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance to Hungarian family and labour-market policy (Belügyminisztérium, EMMI, NGM). The paper documents that pandemic school-closures had persistent, not just temporary, labour-market effects on mothers — implying childcare-disruption shocks have long-lasting consequences. Useful input for childcare-availability policy and for any future pandemic-preparedness planning. Particularly relevant for evaluating the cost-effectiveness of expanded summer-childcare or extended-hours óvoda/iskolai programmes.

title: Corporate governance and the structure of ownership of Hungarian corporations
summary_en: Telegdy surveys the structure of corporate ownership and governance in Hungary in this 2011 country chapter for the Edward Elgar Handbook on International Corporate Governance. He traces the legacy of the 1990s privatisation programme — wide dispersion of ownership in the immediate post-transition period followed by progressive concentration into domestic and foreign blockholders — and reviews the evidence on the link between ownership type and firm performance, board structure, minority-shareholder protection, and the impact of the 2008 crisis on Hungarian listed and unlisted firms.
data_used: Narrative chapter drawing on Hungarian firm-registry data, BÉT (Budapest Stock Exchange) listings, secondary literature on the Hungarian privatisation programme, and Telegdy's own published work on Hungarian corporate ownership and performance up to 2010.
policy_relevance: Background reading for any Hungarian corporate-governance reform (FM/IM company-law amendments, BÉT listing-rules updates, MNB stewardship guidance): summarises what is known about how privatisation choices in the 1990s shaped today's ownership concentration and how that concentration interacts with firm performance. Also relevant for state-asset management (MNV) decisions about when to dispose of remaining state stakes.

title: Public wage spillovers: The role of individual characteristics and employer wage policies
summary_en: Telegdy uses a large unexpected Hungarian public-sector wage increase (the public-wage premium jumped from -17% to +7.5% in 2002 from one month to the next) to causally identify wage spillovers from public to corporate sector. Workers more exposed to the public sector (in their gender-experience-occupation-region segment) saw their corporate-sector wages rise by 9.6 percentage points more between the 25th and 75th exposure percentiles. The firm-level exposure effect is larger (13.6%), suggesting employers respond to anticipated wage tensions. Spillovers concentrate among young, mobile, and highly-educated workers — the groups most likely to switch into the public sector.
data_used: Hungarian linked employer-employee data 2000-2003 covering all formal-sector workers, with detailed individual characteristics (gender, age, occupation, education, region) and firm-level controls; ~millions of worker-firm-year observations.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence for the Pénzügyminisztérium when calibrating public-sector wage increases — corporate-sector spillovers are substantial and concentrated among mobile, educated workers. Useful for budget impact assessments of teacher-wage, nurse-wage, and civil-service-wage increases. Also relevant for MNB inflation-monitoring of public-wage shocks.

title: The effects of enterprise relief grants during COVID-19
summary_en: During COVID-19, Hungary disbursed enterprise relief grants to firms hit by the pandemic. Telegdy uses linked NAV and MVH administrative data to estimate the effect of these grants on firm-level employment and turnover, comparing recipient firms to similar non-recipients via matching. The note documents a positive but modest short-run employment effect concentrated in smaller firms and in sectors with the steepest demand drop, with weaker effects on revenue. [Note-length summary in Economics Letters; an editor-side spot-check against the published version is recommended.]
data_used: Hungarian firm-level administrative panel data (NAV corporate tax filings, employment registers) covering 2019–2021, linked to MVH / NAV grant-disbursement records. Matching estimator on firm size, sector, pre-pandemic trajectory.
policy_relevance: Directly relevant for evaluating future Hungarian crisis-response programmes (MFB / Eximbank emergency lending, AM agri-relief, ITM industrial buffers). Suggests targeting future enterprise-relief instruments at small firms in shock-exposed sectors, where the short-run employment payoff is largest. Provides a concrete Hungarian benchmark for COVID-era programme evaluations now being commissioned by the Állami Számvevőszék.

title: Dynamic branching and interest rate competition of commercial banks: Evidence from Hungary
summary_en: Most bank-competition models take branch networks as given. Temesváry endogenises them — banks choose how many branches to open, and those choices affect interest-rate competition. Applying a dynamic structural model to Hungarian commercial banks 2004-2007, she finds banks charge an interest-rate premium for relative branch-network dominance, and banks with smaller networks are less likely to close branches. The paper derives structural estimates of branch setup costs and scrap values, and shows how branching restrictions could be used as a regulatory tool to alter lending rates and consumer welfare.
data_used: Hungarian bank-level data 2004-2007 from MNB and PSZÁF supervisory reports, covering all commercial banks' branch counts, interest rates by product, and balance-sheet metrics; quarterly observations.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence on Hungarian banking competition. The paper shows banks earn rents on relative branch dominance — relevant for MNB and GVH when evaluating bank-merger applications, branch-closure programmes, and the post-2008 consolidation of the Hungarian banking sector. Also useful for the Pénzügyminisztérium when assessing financial-inclusion concerns from rural branch closures.

title: The drivers of foreign currency‐based banking in Central and Eastern Europe
summary_en: Why did foreign-currency banking spread so quickly across Central and Eastern Europe in 2000-2011, and what can macroprudential policy learn from it? Temesváry uses a new dataset on FX and domestic-currency loans, deposits, and interest rates across 16 CEE countries. Both demand-side (consumer) and supply-side (bank) determinants matter. Three findings: (1) local-FX interest-rate and market-share spreads are lower in managed currency regimes, (2) they are strongly affected by FX-funding prevalence, currency mismatch, and FX banking restrictions, (3) they widen after economic crises. The paper provides the cleanest decomposition to date of the FX-banking phenomenon that became Hungary's biggest macroprudential problem.
data_used: Newly constructed dataset on FX and domestic-currency loans, deposits, and interest rates for 16 CEE countries, 2000-2011. Country-level panel regressions with currency-regime, capital-flow, and crisis controls.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance to MNB macroprudential policy and to Hungarian retrospective analysis of the 2008-2014 FX-mortgage crisis. The paper's finding that FX-banking restrictions matter supports the post-2014 Hungarian regulatory framework that explicitly limited FX household lending. Useful baseline for evaluating CEE-wide macroprudential coordination via the European Systemic Risk Board.

title: The drivers of foreign bank lending in Central and Eastern Europe: The roles of parent, subsidiary and host market traits
summary_en: Western European banks' Central and East European subsidiaries underwent dramatic lending swings during 2008-13. Temesváry and Banai use bank-level data on Western European parent groups and their CEE subsidiaries 2002-2013 to disentangle subsidiary vs. parent drivers of lending. Lower capital ratios and higher non-performing-loan ratios at either level reduced subsidiary lending growth — both before and during the crisis. The crisis weakened the link in many cases, but subsidiaries participating in the Vienna Initiative (2009 commitment to maintain CEE exposures) showed significantly less crisis-driven lending contraction. Policy implications: clean up parent-bank NPLs, coordinate regulation, and include parent traits in countercyclical buffer calculations.
data_used: Bank-level dataset on Western European banking groups (Erste, Raiffeisen, UniCredit, Intesa, KBC, etc.) and their CEE subsidiaries 2002-2013, sourced from Bankscope, MNB, and other CEE central banks, with both parent and subsidiary balance-sheet metrics.
policy_relevance: Highly relevant for Hungarian financial-stability policy. The paper shows Vienna Initiative participation made a measurable difference in subsidiary lending behaviour during the crisis — supporting MNB's continued engagement with such cross-border-coordination platforms. Also informs how Hungarian countercyclical capital buffers should account for parent-bank conditions.

title: Rising between-workplace inequalities in high-income countries
summary_en: When inequality rises, where does it come from — within-firm differences (top managers versus rank-and-file) or between-firm differences (some companies pay more than others)? This paper uses comprehensive administrative records for 14 high-income countries to decompose the trend. The between-workplace component grows in almost every country examined and declines in none. Within-workplace inequality's trend varies. The finding has profound policy implications: policies aimed at within-firm pay structures will increasingly miss the growing source of inequality. Firm-level productivity and labour-market sorting dynamics become the right focal points.
data_used: Administrative linked employer-employee records for 14 high-income countries covering 2 billion+ job-years and 50 million+ workplaces. Hungary included via Boza and Hajdu contributions.
policy_relevance: Central for understanding Hungarian wage-inequality trends and for policy design. The paper's key message — between-firm inequality is rising everywhere — shifts policy attention to: firm-size policy, sector-specific productivity policy, minimum-wage design across firms, and collective-bargaining coverage. Relevant to MNB wage analysis, VKF social dialogue, and Ministry of Economy wage-policy design. Caveat: the measurement focuses on high-income-country experience; Hungarian-specific decomposition should be done on KRTK data.

title: A köztisztviselői törvények hatása a kormányzati kiadásokra
summary_en: Ujhelyi reviews the question of whether bureaucracy should be insulated from politics — and what economic and political-science research has learned about the consequences of civil-service legislation that strengthens or weakens that insulation. Drawing on his own US-based work and the broader international literature, he covers the trade-offs civil-service rules impose on the interaction between politicians, voters, and bureaucrats; the empirical evidence on government-spending effects of merit-based recruitment; and the implications for emerging democracies. The piece is a Hungarian-language synthesis that brings the international debate into the domestic policy conversation.
data_used: Literature review covering US, OECD, and emerging-democracy evidence on civil-service rules and their effects on government spending and policy choices.
policy_relevance: Hungarian-language synthesis specifically aimed at Hungarian policy audiences. Direct relevance for the Belügyminisztérium, the Public Service Commission, and the Magyar Közigazgatási Karok during ongoing reforms of the legal status of public servants. Provides accessible context for Hungarian policymakers reading the international literature.

title: Household debt revaluation and the real economy: Evidence from a foreign currency debt crisis
summary_en: When the Hungarian forint collapsed in late 2008, households holding Swiss-franc and euro mortgages saw their debt service jump 30-50%. Verner and Gyöngyösi exploit cross-region variation in foreign-currency-mortgage exposure to causally estimate the impact on the local economy. Affected districts experienced higher default rates, collapsed consumption spending, and deeper recessions — even spilling over to nearby borrowers without FX debt. The implied output multiplier on debt-service shocks is 1.67. Crucially, the impact was much worse when FX debt was on household rather than firm balance sheets.
data_used: Hungarian regional administrative records on household foreign-currency mortgage exposure (MNB, ÁKK), default outcomes, household consumption (KSH), and local labour-market outcomes by district 2008-2014.
policy_relevance: Foundational evidence for Hungarian macroprudential policy at MNB. The paper demonstrates household-FX-debt risks are systemically larger than firm-FX-debt risks — directly informing MNB's 2014 conversion of the FX-mortgage stock into forint and ongoing macroprudential limits. Also relevant for the Pénzügyminisztérium and other Eastern European central banks (NBR, NBP, NBS) addressing similar legacy stocks.

title: Kezelési költségük határozza-e meg a Magyarországon forgalmazott részvénypiaci befektetési alapok teljesítményét?
summary_en: Do management fees explain mutual-fund performance in Hungary? Zawadowski tests this on Hungarian-marketed equity funds. The baseline specification finds that a 1-percentage-point higher management fee corresponds to *more than* 1 percentage point worse performance versus benchmark (Jensen's alpha) — a striking failure of the cost-quality relationship in mutual funds. He shows that several funds officially marketed as actively managed in fact track an index. He also documents measurement difficulties: the BÉT-created CETOP benchmark index excludes dividends, which biases performance comparisons; he proposes how to correct this. A clean Hungarian application of the international 'fees don't deliver alpha' literature.
data_used: Hungarian-marketed equity mutual fund returns and management-fee data. Sample period covers a recent multi-year window. CETOP and other benchmark-index data from BÉT. Jensen's alpha calculations across the fund universe.
policy_relevance: Direct input for MNB consumer-protection oversight of Hungarian retail investment funds. The paper provides empirical foundation for fee-disclosure rules and for warning retail investors about active-tracking-passive ('closet indexing') funds. Useful for the Hungarian fund-industry debate about transparency standards. The CETOP-index dividend issue should inform Hungarian regulatory choices about benchmark methodology.

title: A comparison of European, Polish, Slovenian and British EQ-5D-3L value sets using a Hungarian sample of 18 chronic diseases
summary_en: The EQ-5D-3L instrument measures health-state utility for cost-effectiveness analysis. But the "value set" (which assigns utility to each state) can differ across countries. Does the choice matter for concrete policy decisions? This paper compares European, Polish, Slovenian, and British value sets on a Hungarian sample of patients with 18 chronic diseases. The conclusion: value-set choice substantially influences health-state utility results in chronic disease — and thus affects health-policy decisions. An important methodological caution for Hungarian cost-effectiveness analyses.
data_used: Hungarian sample of patients with 18 chronic diseases, evaluated against European, Polish, Slovenian, and British EQ-5D-3L value sets.
policy_relevance: Directly relevant to Hungarian health-technology assessment (GYEMSZI, NEAK) and to drug-reimbursement decisions. The paper supports the development of a Hungarian-specific value set for EQ-5D-3L to avoid systematic biases from using foreign sets. Relevant to Hungarian HTA methodology reform. Caveat: chronic-disease focus; acute and preventive-care implications may differ.
